title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
今上御極之十有二年為弘治己
未天下士會試于禮部者三
千五百人
上命臣東陽臣敏政為考試官先
事以請者尚書臣寬侍郎臣
瀚臣昇同考試則為修撰臣
===

會試錄序

今上御極之十有二年，為弘治己未，天下士會試于禮部者三千五百人。上命臣東陽、臣敏政為考試官。先事以請者，尚書臣寬、侍郎臣瀚、臣昇。同考試則為修撰臣春、贊善臣宏、編修臣冕、臣穆、臣清、臣一鵬、臣費、臣韶、臣詠、都給事中臣廷玉、給事中臣士賢、郎中臣莊、員外郎臣瓚、主事臣爟。監試則為御史臣茂、臣獻民，暨諸執事，慎簡備集，皆如
translation_en:
Preface to the Metropolitan Examination Record

The twelfth year since the present emperor ascended the throne was the jiwei year of the Hongzhi reign [1499]. Three thousand five hundred scholars from throughout the realm assembled at the Ministry of Rites for the Metropolitan Examination. His Majesty appointed your servants Dongyang and Minzheng as Examiners. The request had been submitted beforehand by your servants Kuan, Minister, and Han and Sheng, Vice Ministers.

The Associate Examiners were your servants Chun, Senior Compiler; Hong, Admonisher; Mian, Mu, Qing, Yipeng, Fei, Shao, and Yong, Junior Compilers; Tingyu, Chief Supervising Secretary; Shixian, Supervising Secretary; Zhuang, Director; Zan, Vice Director; and Guan, Secretary. title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
制癸丑之試臣東陽實典試事
嘗盡觀天下之文今乃獲再
至再觀其所謂文者校諸曩
歲有加焉為之目眩心動累
日不置擇其純以俟
宸斷得三百人其限于
制額而不能悉取者盖亦多矣
===
乃相與歎曰文之盛一至此
哉夫文之在人實關乎行在
天下則政治繫之我
國家天造之初氣化渾厚歷數
十年漸以宣朗又數十年而
條制之精明典儀之賁飾已
極故文之於科舉亦然洪武
alt_text:
制癸丑之試〔曰東詔〕實典試事
嘗盡觀天下之文今乃獲再
至再觀其所謂文者校諸曩
歲有加焉爲之目眩心動累
日不置擇其純以俟
宸斷得三百人其限于
制額而不能悉取者蓋亦多矣
===
乃相與歎曰文之盛一至此
哉夫文之在人實關乎行在
天下則政治繫之我
國家天造之初氣化渾厚歷數
十年漸以宣朗又數十年而
條制之精明典儀之賁飾已
極故文之於科舉亦然洪武
punctuated:
制。癸丑之試，臣東陽實典試事，嘗盡觀天下之文。今乃獲再至，再觀其所謂文者，校諸曩歲，有加焉，為之目眩心動，累日不置。擇其純以俟宸斷，得三百人。其限于制額而不能悉取者，盖亦多矣。
乃相與歎曰：「文之盛，一至此哉！」夫文之在人，實關乎行；在天下，則政治繫之。我國家天造之初，氣化渾厚，歷數十年，漸以宣朗；又數十年，而條制之精明、典儀之賁飾已極。故文之於科舉亦然。洪武
translation_en:
…the prescribed regulations. At the examination of the guichou year [1493], I, your servant Dongyang, was in charge of the examination and had occasion to survey the writings of candidates from throughout the realm. Now, having had the opportunity to return and examine their writings once more, I find that they surpass those of former years. They dazzled my eyes and stirred my heart; for days on end I could not put them down. We selected those of unalloyed excellence to await Your Majesty’s judgment, obtaining three hundred men. Yet there were surely many more whom the prescribed quota prevented us from accepting.
Together we sighed in admiration, saying: “Has literary accomplishment reached such heights!” In an individual, literary accomplishment is indeed bound up with conduct; in the realm as a whole, government is tied to it. At the Heaven-ordained founding of our dynasty, the transforming vital forces were rich and substantial. Over several decades they gradually unfolded into clarity; after several more decades, the refinement and clarity of regulations and the splendid elaboration of rites and ceremonies had reached their utmost. The same has therefore been true of writing in the civil-service examinations. In the Hongwu era…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
永樂之製簡而不遺質而成
章迄于今日屢出屢變愈趨
于盛然議經析理細入秋豪
而大義或畧役意造語爭竒
鬪博惟陳言之務去而正氣
或不充若必如是而後可以
為文則其論議識見見諸猷
===
為著於事業於
朝廷天下者視前輩何如也故
文之極盛亦識治體者之所
慎也是寧獨士之責哉典教
之官惟程課是急司考校者
操尺寸以臨之而於大且正
者鮮加之意故其為法雖精
alt_text:

章迄于今日屢出屢變愈趨
于盛然議經析理細入秋豪
而大義或畧發意造語爭奇
鬭博惟陳言之務去而正氣
或不充若必如是而後可以
為文則其論議識見見諸猷
===
為著於事業於
朝廷天下者視前輩何如也故
文之極盛亦識治體者之所
慎也是寧獨士之責哉典教
之官惟程課是急司考校者
操尺寸以臨之而於大且正
者鮮加之意故其為法雖精
punctuated: 永樂之製，簡而不遺，質而成章。迄于今日，屢出屢變，愈趨于盛。然議經析理，細入秋豪，而大義或畧；役意造語，爭竒鬪博，惟陳言之務去，而正氣或不充。若必如是而後可以為文，則其論議識見，見諸猷為，著於事業，於朝廷天下者，視前輩何如也？故文之極盛，亦識治體者之所慎也。是寧獨士之責哉？典教之官，惟程課是急；司考校者，操尺寸以臨之，而於大且正者鮮加之意。故其為法雖精，
translation_en: …and Yongle reigns were concise without omissions, plain yet well composed. Down to the present day, successive works have brought successive changes, and writing has flourished ever more. Yet in discussing the Classics and analyzing principles, writers pursue subtleties as fine as an autumn hair, while sometimes neglecting the greater meaning. They strain their minds to fashion phrases, competing in novelty and vying in erudition, intent only on eliminating familiar expressions, while their writing sometimes lacks an ample spirit of rectitude. If writing must be like this before it can count as literary composition, then how do their arguments and insights, manifested in plans and actions and expressed in accomplishments at court and throughout the realm, compare with those of their predecessors? Thus even the utmost flourishing of writing is something those who understand the essentials of governance regard with caution. Can this be the responsibility of scholars alone? Officials charged with education concern themselves urgently only with prescribed assignments; those responsible for examining and assessing apply narrow measures to the candidates, giving little attention to what is substantial and upright. Thus, although their methods are meticulous, …

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
而顧不能無弊亦勢使之然
也昔人有言先王質文相變
以濟天下質敝則佐之以文
文敝則復之以質
聖天子方法
祖宗監
成憲挈一世之文而敺之以復
===
于舊
意嚮所示盖自求真才始諸士
子錄于有司方藉是以進尚
以其素所學者躬體而踐之
俾官有定守言有確論功有
著業不獨於文之純而止要
其成自

而顧不能無弊亦勢使之然
也昔人有言先王質文相變
以濟天下質敝則佐之以文
文敝則復之以質
聖天子方法
祖宗監
成憲挈一世之文而毆之以復
===
于舊
宸衷所示蓋自求真才始諸士
子錄于有司方藉是以進尚
以其素所學者躬體而踐之
俾官有定守言有確論功有
著業不獨於文之純而止要
其成自
punctuated: 而顧不能無弊，亦勢使之然也。昔人有言：「先王質文相變以濟天下，質敝則佐之以文，文敝則復之以質。」聖天子方法祖宗，監成憲，挈一世之文而敺之以復于舊。意嚮所示，盖自求真才始。諸士子錄于有司，方藉是以進，尚以其素所學者躬體而踐之，俾官有定守，言有確論，功有著業，不獨於文之純而止。要其成，自
translation_en: …yet it cannot be free of defects; circumstances themselves make this so. Someone of old said: “The former kings alternated substance and refinement to bring order to the world. When substance became worn out, they supplemented it with refinement; when refinement became worn out, they returned to substance.” The sagely Son of Heaven is now modeling himself on his ancestors and taking their established statutes as his guide, leading the literary culture of the age back to its former standards. The direction indicated by his intentions begins, it would seem, with seeking genuine talent. You scholars, selected by the responsible officials and now advancing by this means, should personally embody and put into practice what you have always studied. Let your service in office have firm principles, your words sound judgments, and your achievements manifest themselves in tangible undertakings; do not stop merely at purity of literary expression. As for the fulfillment of these aims, from…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
朝廷達于天下無所往而弗效
則斯文者庶幾實用乎世而
非徒盛也且唐虞之代敷奏
考言期於底績漢之制策往
往見之于行唐宋以科舉取
士而韓愈程顥者出焉其闢
邪扶正明聖道開來學之功
===
乃世之所以為重文之實用
固如此
國家教試既純乎經文之盛又
將復而之古若二子者豈無
其人臣不佞與有以人事
君之責今日之事亦裨益
聖治之端也其敢不慎以求之第
alt_text:
朝廷達于天下無所往而弗效
則斯文者庶幾實用乎世而
非徒盛也且唐虞之代敷奏
考言期於底績漢之制策往
往見之于行唐宋以科舉取
士而韓愈程顥者出焉其闢
邪扶正明聖道開來學之功
乃世之所以為重文之實用
國如此
===
國家教試既純乎經文之盛又
將復而之古若二子者豈無
其人〔臣〕不佞與有以人事
君之責今日之事亦裨益
聖治之端也其敢不慎以求之第
punctuated:
朝廷達于天下，無所往而弗效，則斯文者庶幾實用乎世，而非徒盛也。且唐虞之代，敷奏考言，期於底績；漢之制策，往往見之于行；唐宋以科舉取士，而韓愈、程顥者出焉。其闢邪扶正、明聖道、開來學之功，乃世之所以為重。文之實用，固如此。
國家教試既純乎經，文之盛又將復而之古，若二子者，豈無其人？臣不佞，與有以人事君之責，今日之事，亦裨益聖治之端也。其敢不慎以求之？第
translation_en:
…from the imperial court throughout the realm, proving effective wherever applied, then this literary learning may indeed serve a practical purpose in the world, rather than merely flourish. Moreover, in the age of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, officials presented their reports and their words were examined, with the aim of achieving results. The policy questions issued by imperial command under the Han often found expression in practice. The Tang and Song selected officials through the civil-service examinations, and men such as Han Yu and Cheng Hao emerged. Their achievements in refuting heterodoxy and upholding orthodoxy, elucidating the Way of the sages and opening the path for future learners, are what the world esteems. Such, indeed, is the practical usefulness of literary learning.
Now that the state's instruction and examinations are grounded exclusively in the Classics, the flourishing of literary learning will also return toward antiquity. Could there be no men like those two masters? Your untalented servant shares the responsibility of serving his sovereign by finding worthy men. The undertaking today is also a means of contributing to Your Majesty's sagely governance. How could I dare be anything but scrupulous in seeking them? Yet…

免遺才之憾爾

書兼文淵閣大學士李東陽
謹序

愧無陸贄、歐陽脩之明，終未免遺才之憾爾。
資政大夫、太子少保、禮部尚書兼文淵閣大學士李東陽謹序。
translation_en:
…I am ashamed that I lack the discernment of Lu Zhi and Ouyang Xiu, and in the end cannot escape the regret of having overlooked worthy talent.
This preface is respectfully composed by Li Dongyang, Grand Master for Assisting in Government, Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Rites, and concurrently Grand Secretary of the Wenyuan Pavilion.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Twelfth Year of Hongzhi (1499)

Xu Qiong, Grand Master for Aid in Governance, Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent, and Minister of Rites. His courtesy name was Shiyong; he was from Jinxi County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the dingchou year (1457).

第壹場

四書

欲罷不能，既竭吾才，如有所立卓爾，雖欲從之，末由也已。

知所以脩身，則知所以治人；知所以治人，則知所以治天下國家矣。凡為天下國家有九經，曰：脩身也，尊賢也，親親也，敬大臣也，體群臣也，子庶民也，来百工也，柔遠人也，懷諸侯也。

惻隱之心，仁也；羞惡之心，義也；恭敬之心，禮也；是非之心，智也。

易

包荒，得尚于中行，以光大也。

說以先民，民忘其勞。

過此以往，未之或知也。窮神知化，德之盛也。

夫乾，天下之至健也，德行恒易以知險；夫坤，天下之至順也，德行恒簡以知阻。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Though I wish to stop, I cannot. Having exhausted all my abilities, I seem to see something standing loftily before me. Though I wish to follow it, I have no way to do so.

Knowing how to cultivate oneself, one knows how to govern others; knowing how to govern others, one knows how to govern the world, its states, and its families. There are nine constant principles for governing the world, its states, and its families: cultivating oneself; honoring the worthy; cherishing one's kin; respecting the great ministers; showing consideration for the body of officials; treating the common people as one's children; attracting the various artisans; treating people from afar with kindness; and cherishing the feudal lords.

The heart of compassion is benevolence; the heart of shame and aversion is righteousness; the heart of reverence and respect is ritual propriety; the heart that distinguishes right from wrong is wisdom.

Book of Changes (Yi)

To embrace what is uncultivated and attain accord with the middle course is possible through breadth and illumination.

Lead the people with joy, and the people forget their toil.

Beyond this point, none has yet known. To fathom the numinous and understand transformation is the fullness of virtue.

Qian is the utmost strength in the world; its virtuous activity is ever easy, enabling it to apprehend danger. Kun is the utmost compliance in the world; its virtuous activity is ever simple, enabling it to apprehend obstruction.

書

嘉言罔攸伏，野無遺賢，萬邦咸寧。稽于衆，舍己從人，不虐無告，不廢困窮。

德無常師，主善為師；善無常主，協于克一。

今王惟曰：「先王既勤用明德，懷為夾，庶邦享，作兄弟方來。亦既用明德，后式典集，庶邦丕享。皇天既付中國民越厥疆土于先王，肆王惟德用，和懌先後迷民，用懌先王受命。」已！若兹監，惟曰：「欲至于萬年，惟王子子孫孫永保民。」

斯謀斯猷，惟我后之德。

詩

孑孑干旌，在浚之城。素絲祝之，良馬六之。彼姝者子，何以告之？

織文鳥章，白旆央央。元戎十乘，以先啓行。

戎車既安，如輊如軒。四牡既佶，既佶且閑。薄伐獫狁，至于大原。

昊天曰明，及爾出王；昊天曰旦，及爾游衍。
translation_en:
Book of Documents

No worthy words remained hidden, and no worthy men were overlooked in the countryside; the myriad states were all at peace. He consulted the multitude, set aside his own views and followed others, did not oppress those with no one to appeal to, and did not neglect the distressed and impoverished.

In cultivating virtue, there is no fixed teacher: take goodness as your teacher. Goodness has no fixed embodiment: accord with an undivided purpose.

Now let the king say: “The former kings diligently put their luminous virtue into practice, winning men over to serve as helpers [?]. The various states presented offerings, and those treated as brothers came from every quarter. Through the practice of luminous virtue, the sovereign thus presided over their gathering, and the various states presented abundant offerings. August Heaven entrusted the people of the central states and their territories to the former kings. Therefore let the king employ virtue, bringing harmony and joy to the misguided people, guiding and supporting them, and thereby bringing joy to the former kings who received the Mandate.” Ah! Taking this as a mirror, let him say: “If our rule is to last ten thousand years, let the king’s sons and grandsons forever protect the people.”

These plans and these counsels manifest our sovereign’s virtue.

Book of Odes

Tall stands the banner on its pole at the city of Jun. White silk cords bind it; fine horses number six. That admirable gentleman—what shall I tell him?

Woven patterns bear bird emblems; white streamers flutter grandly. Ten great war chariots lead the way and open the march.

The war chariots are steady, now tilting forward, now rising. The four stallions are sturdy, sturdy and well trained. We marched against the Xianyun, reaching as far as Dayuan.

Vast Heaven is bright, watching you as you go forth; vast Heaven is radiant, watching you as you roam at leisure.

When instruction begins in the Great Learning, the students wear leather caps and offer vegetables in sacrifice, thereby showing reverence for the Way. They rehearse three poems from the Minor Odes, thus beginning their preparation for official service. Upon entering the school, they open their book boxes at the beating of the drum, thereby submitting themselves to their studies. The two kinds of rods, of catalpa and thornwood, maintain their proper awe. Until divination has been performed for the di sacrifice, there is no inspection of the school, allowing their aspirations free play. The teacher observes them at appropriate times without speaking, preserving their attentiveness. Younger students listen without asking questions: learning does not skip stages.

問：古昔帝王創業垂統，必有謨訓傳之家邦。我太祖高皇帝立法定制，製為祖訓，以遺東宮、親王；又命編輯前代善惡為《昭鑒錄》，以賜諸王。盖重根本、蕃枝葉，為億萬載隆長之計。其視法術之賜、詩書之教、帝範之作、開元之訓、仁孝之詩、麟趾之篇，以至承華之有畧、元良之有述，萬萬不侔矣。是書雖蔵在秘府，而見諸聖政之記、儒臣所叙述者，天下固已傳之。諸士子亦嘗習聞而與知乎？聞而知之，請述
translation_en:
Submitting an anonymous document accusing someone of a crime.

Third Session
Five Policy Questions

Question: When the emperors and kings of antiquity founded their enterprises and established a succession, they invariably left counsels and instructions for their ruling houses and realms. Our Emperor Taizu Gao established laws and fixed institutions, composing the Ancestral Instructions to bequeath to the heir apparent and the imperial princes. He also commanded that examples of good and evil from earlier ages be compiled as the Record of Illuminating Admonitions (Zhaojian lu) and bestowed upon the princes. This was a plan to strengthen the roots and make the branches and leaves flourish, ensuring enduring prosperity for countless ages. Compared with earlier bestowals of methods of government, instruction through the Odes and Documents, the composition of the Model for Emperors (Di fan), the instructions of the Kaiyuan era, poems on benevolence and filial piety, the “Unicorn’s Hoof” (Lin zhi) piece, and even the Outline for the Heir Apparent (Chenghua lüe) and the Account for the Heir Apparent (Yuanliang shu), these provisions were beyond all comparison.

Although this book is stored in the palace archives, those portions appearing in records of the imperial administration and in accounts by Confucian officials have already circulated throughout the realm. Have you candidates also heard them often and come to understand them? If you have heard and understood them, please set forth …

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
聖祖之鴻猷大旨以為天下告則於
明天子端本睦親之治不為無補也
問天下之治存乎紀綱而成乎風俗斯二
者果相須邪亦各自為用而不能相通
邪且二者之名起於何時二者之義何
所於取漢唐宋之所以為紀綱者何如
所以為風俗者何如其安危治亂可考
而知也言紀綱者莫切於韓昌黎朱晦
菴彼論議之士或以賞罰或以官爵或
===
以法度或以井田其為說孰要乎言風
俗者莫切於賈誼陸贄彼循行之典或
詔公卿大夫或令二千石或遣諫官博
士或太中大夫其為法孰善乎

賞而勸不罰而治不令而行不教而聽

punctuated:
聖祖之鴻猷大旨，以為天下告，則於明天子端本睦親之治，不為無補也。

問：天下之治，存乎紀綱而成乎風俗。斯二者果相須邪？亦各自為用而不能相通邪？且二者之名起於何時？二者之義何所於取？漢唐宋之所以為紀綱者何如？所以為風俗者何如？其安危治亂，可考而知也。言紀綱者莫切於韓昌黎、朱晦菴，彼論議之士，或以賞罰，或以官爵，或以法度，或以井田，其為說孰要乎？言風俗者莫切於賈誼、陸贄，彼循行之典，或詔公卿大夫，或令二千石，或遣諫官博士，或太中大夫，其為法孰善乎？國朝統御之初，紀綱振肅，風俗齊一，遠過前代。然歲久勢殊，未免有偏而不起之處。茲號令詳悉，條格具備，而捄偏補敝、返朴還淳之效，猶或未臻。不知古之人不賞而勸，不罰而治，不令而行，不教而聽
translation_en:
…the grand designs and central purposes of the Sagely Founder, making them known to all under Heaven. This would be of some assistance to the enlightened Son of Heaven’s governance in rectifying the root and fostering harmony among his imperial kinsmen.

Question: Order throughout the realm rests upon governing principles and institutions and is brought to completion through social customs. Do these two indeed depend upon each other? Or does each function independently, without any connection between them? Moreover, when did these two terms originate, and from what were their meanings derived? What constituted governing principles and institutions under the Han, Tang, and Song? What shaped their social customs? Their security and peril, order and disorder, can be understood through investigation. Among those who discussed governing principles and institutions, none spoke more pointedly than Han Changli and Zhu Hui’an. Among those who debated these matters, some emphasized rewards and punishments, some offices and ranks, some laws and regulations, and some the well-field system. Which explanation best grasps the essentials? Among those who discussed social customs, none spoke more pointedly than Jia Yi and Lu Zhi. As for the established practices of inspection tours, sometimes edicts were addressed to dukes, ministers, and grandees; sometimes orders were issued to officials ranked at two thousand bushels; sometimes remonstrance officials and erudites were dispatched, or grand masters of the palace. Which method was best?

When our dynasty first assumed rule, governing principles and institutions were vigorously enforced, and social customs were brought into concord, far surpassing previous dynasties. Yet as the years passed and circumstances changed, there inevitably arose areas of imbalance that failed to recover. Now commands and ordinances are detailed and comprehensive, and regulations are fully provided, yet the desired results of correcting imbalances, remedying abuses, and restoring simplicity and sincerity have perhaps still not been attained. We do not understand how the people of antiquity encouraged others without rewards, maintained order without punishments, secured action without commands, and obtained obedience without instruction…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
何以能然也有志於世道者寧可黙焉
而已乎
問學者於前賢之所造詣非問之審辨之
明則無所據以得師而為歸宿之地矣
試舉其大者言之有講道于西與程子
相望而興者或謂其似伯夷有載道而
南得程子相傳之的者或謂其似展季
有致力于存心養性專師孟子者或疑
其出於禪有從事于小學大學私淑朱
===
子者或疑其出於老夫此四公皆所謂
豪傑之士曠世而見者其造道之地乃
不一如此後學亦徒因古人之成說謂
其然爾真知其似伯夷似展季疑於禪
疑於老者果何在邪請極論之以觀平
日之所嘗究心者
問政有名有實名與實應則治成故忠信
誠慤可以結民虛偽誣罔不可以為化
昔人有是言矣自省成考課之法弊在

punctuated:
何以能然也？有志於世道者，寧可黙焉而已乎？

問：學者於前賢之所造詣，非問之審、辨之明，則無所據以得師而為歸宿之地矣。試舉其大者言之：有講道于西，與程子相望而興者，或謂其似伯夷；有載道而南，得程子相傳之的者，或謂其似展季；有致力于存心養性，專師孟子者，或疑其出於禪；有從事于小學大學，私淑朱子者，或疑其出於老。夫此四公，皆所謂豪傑之士，曠世而見者，其造道之地，乃不一如此。後學亦徒因古人之成說，謂其然爾。真知其似伯夷、似展季、疑於禪、疑於老者，果何在邪？請極論之，以觀平日之所嘗究心者。

問：政有名有實，名與實應則治成。故忠信誠慤可以結民，虛偽誣罔不可以為化，昔人有是言矣。自省成考課之法，弊在
translation_en:
…how were they able to achieve this? Can those committed to the moral order of the world simply remain silent?

Question: Unless students inquire carefully into the attainments of former worthies and distinguish them clearly, they will have no basis for finding a teacher and establishing a firm destination for their learning. Let us select the principal examples for discussion. One taught the Way in the west and rose to prominence alongside Master Cheng; some say he resembled Bo Yi. One carried the Way southward and obtained the authentic teaching transmitted by Master Cheng; some say he resembled Zhan Ji. One devoted his efforts to preserving the mind and nurturing the nature, taking Mencius alone as his teacher; some suspect that his teaching derived from Chan Buddhism. One applied himself to the Elementary Learning and the Great Learning, taking Master Zhu as his teacher through his transmitted teachings; some suspect that his teaching derived from Laozi. These four gentlemen were all what are called outstanding men, appearing only once in many generations. Yet their attainments in the Way differed to this extent. Later students merely follow the established judgments of earlier men and repeat that these are so. Where, precisely, is the basis for truly knowing that they resembled Bo Yi or Zhan Ji, or for suspecting affinities with Chan Buddhism or Laozi? Discuss this fully, so that we may see what you have habitually studied with care.

Question: Government has both name and substance. When name corresponds to substance, good government is achieved. Thus loyalty, trustworthiness, sincerity, and honesty can bind the people together, while falsehood, deceit, misrepresentation, and deception cannot bring about moral transformation. Men of former times have said this. As for the methods of reviewing accomplishments and evaluating officials’ performance, their abuses lay in …

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
漢或綜核名實而計簿欺謾戶口增偽
或責課公卿而屯田警備失實者多在
唐或銳意治功而邊鎮交兵器械幾盡
在宋或躬親庶政裁抑僥倖而用刑行
政審官納諫之實猶有議焉彼皆願治
之君而名實之不相應如此然則將聽
其所為而終莫能正邪抑別有其道也
今天下之政名存而實弊者不可僂數
必欲使上下惇信內外孚感終始貞固
===
復古道於數千載之上不可謂不難矣
試與諸士子圖之
問民為邦本而兵所以為國禦侮有天下
者庸可不加之意乎我
太祖高皇帝御極惠民養兵度越前古其在當
時民安于供賦而樂兵堅于捍衛而嬉
可謂盛矣承平既久民之版籍猶昔也
然轉徙者未能招來山澤所藏或有他
虞將何以處之兵之尺伍猶昔也然逃

punctuated:
漢，或綜核名實，而計簿欺謾，戶口增偽；或責課公卿，而屯田警備失實者多。在唐，或銳意治功，而邊鎮交兵，器械幾盡。在宋，或躬親庶政，裁抑僥倖，而用刑行政、審官納諫之實，猶有議焉。彼皆願治之君，而名實之不相應如此，然則將聽其所為，而終莫能正邪？抑別有其道也？今天下之政，名存而實弊者，不可僂數。必欲使上下惇信，內外孚感，終始貞固，復古道於數千載之上，不可謂不難矣。試與諸士子圖之。

問：民為邦本，而兵所以為國禦侮，有天下者庸可不加之意乎？我太祖高皇帝御極，惠民養兵，度越前古。其在當時，民安于供賦而樂，兵堅于捍衛而嬉，可謂盛矣。承平既久，民之版籍猶昔也，然轉徙者未能招來，山澤所藏或有他虞，將何以處之？兵之尺伍猶昔也，然逃
translation_en:
…under the Han, some rulers comprehensively scrutinized names and actual performance, yet the accounting registers were deceptive and household and population figures were falsely inflated. Others held the highest officials accountable for their performance, yet military agricultural colonies and defensive preparations frequently fell short of what was reported. Under the Tang, some rulers earnestly pursued effective government, yet frontier garrisons fought one another, and their weapons and equipment were nearly exhausted. Under the Song, some rulers personally attended to the many affairs of government and curbed the pursuit of unmerited favors, yet their actual performance in applying punishments, administering government, evaluating officials, and accepting remonstrance remained open to criticism. These were all rulers who desired good government, yet the discrepancy between name and reality was such as this. Must one then let them act as they please, ultimately unable to rectify matters? Or is there another way?

Today, the affairs of government throughout the realm in which the name survives but the substance has deteriorated are too numerous to count. To ensure that superiors and subordinates alike cultivate trustworthiness, that those at court and in the provinces respond to one another with sincerity, and that all remain steadfast from beginning to end, thereby restoring the ancient Way of several thousand years ago—this cannot be called easy. Let the candidates consider how it might be accomplished.

Question: The people are the foundation of the state, while soldiers are the means by which the state resists aggression. Can anyone who rules the realm possibly fail to give these matters attention? When our Emperor Taizu Gao ascended the throne, his beneficence toward the people and provision for the soldiers surpassed those of earlier ages. In his time, the people were content and happy to supply their taxes, and the soldiers were steadfast and cheerful in defending the realm. This may indeed be called a flourishing age.

After so long a period of peace, the household registers remain as they were before. Yet those who have moved away have not been induced to return, and those concealed in the mountains and marshes may give rise to other concerns. How should this be dealt with? The military ranks remain as they were before, yet those who flee…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
亡者莫可究詰戰守所繋恒有隱憂將
何以捄之
列聖以来增有司以撫民其惠亦周矣何版籍
之卒難于復也責憲臣以清軍其法亦
嚴矣何尺伍之卒難于充也豈均需太
重不能懇減有假託以為利者乎抑公
作頻繁不能加恤有並緣以自殖者乎
江南之民雖若稍裕然課辦多矣設有
歉歲孰為之繼三邊之兵雖若素整然
===
役戍疲矣脫有警報孰任其責此皆
宵旰之慮當路者所欲聞也如使民復而内
以實兵足而外以固必有道焉諸士子
宜悉所蘊以對

===
役戍疲矣脫有警報孰任其責此皆
宵旰之慮當路者所欲聞也如使民復而內
以實兵足而外以固必有道焉諸士子
宜悉所蘊以對
punctuated: 亡者莫可究詰，戰守所繋，恒有隱憂，將何以捄之？列聖以来，增有司以撫民，其惠亦周矣，何版籍之卒難于復也？責憲臣以清軍，其法亦嚴矣，何尺伍之卒難于充也？豈均需太重，不能懇減，有假託以為利者乎？抑公作頻繁，不能加恤，有並緣以自殖者乎？江南之民雖若稍裕，然課辦多矣，設有歉歲，孰為之繼？三邊之兵雖若素整，然役戍疲矣，脫有警報，孰任其責？此皆宵旰之慮，當路者所欲聞也。如使民復而内以實，兵足而外以固，必有道焉。諸士子宜悉所蘊以對。
translation_en:
…those who have deserted cannot be traced or called to account. In matters bearing upon warfare and defense, hidden anxieties persist. How can this be remedied? Since the reigns of our successive sage emperors, additional officials have been appointed to care for the people, and their beneficence has been comprehensive. Why, then, has it remained so difficult to restore the population registers? Censors have been charged with rectifying the military rolls, and the regulations have been strict. Why, then, has it remained so difficult to fill the ranks? Could it be that apportioned requisitions [?] are too heavy and cannot be reduced in earnest [?], while some use them as a pretext for private gain? Or is it that public works are frequent, relief cannot be provided, and some exploit these circumstances to enrich themselves [?]?

Although the people of Jiangnan appear somewhat prosperous, their tax and supply obligations are numerous. Should a year of poor harvests occur, who would sustain them? Although the troops of the Three Border Commands appear ordinarily well ordered, they are exhausted by labor service and garrison duty. Should an alarm suddenly arise, who would bear responsibility? These are all concerns that keep His Majesty occupied before dawn and late into the night, and matters on which those in authority wish to hear your views. There must be a way to restore the population and thereby strengthen the realm internally, and to bring the troops to full strength and thereby secure it externally. You candidates should set forth all that you have learned and considered in your replies.

從之末由也已

第壹塲

四書

「欲罷不能，既竭吾才，如有所立卓爾。雖欲從之，末由也已。」

周塤

同考試官郎中邵批：顏子學之所至，體認親切，無喻此篇。

同考試官編修賈批：顏子學有得處，正不易言。此作從容數語便妙，豈亦學顏而有得者歟？

同考試官編修濮批：體貼顏子善學聖人處，親切有味，非苟作者。

同考試官編修顧批：於顏子不容致力之地，而能以文字形容之，亦可以見其所造矣。

考試官學士程批：平易中極有理趣，似非專于辭者。

考試官大學士李批：說見道處，語意甚活，定非穉筆可到。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Though I wish to stop, I cannot. Having exhausted my abilities, I seem to see something standing loftily before me. Though I wish to follow it, I have no means of doing so.”

Zhou Xun

Comment by Associate Examiner Shao, Director: In its intimate understanding of the point Master Yan reached in his learning, nothing compares with this essay [?].

Comment by Associate Examiner Jia, Compiler: What Master Yan attained through learning is indeed difficult to express. This composition achieves subtlety with a few unhurried words. Could its author also have gained something by learning from Yan?

Comment by Associate Examiner Pu, Compiler: Its sympathetic understanding of how Master Yan excelled at learning from the Sage is intimate and rich in meaning. This is no careless composition.

Comment by Associate Examiner Gu, Compiler: The author can describe in words the point at which Master Yan could exert no further effort. This also reveals the level the author himself has attained.

Comment by Examiner Cheng, Academician: Beneath its plain and accessible language lies a profound appreciation of principle. The author seems concerned with more than wording alone.

Comment by Examiner Li, Grand Secretary: In explaining the point at which the Way is perceived, the language and meaning are exceptionally vivid. This is certainly beyond the reach of an immature writer.

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
大賢悅聖道之深而盡其力見聖道之的而難
為功盖道可以力求不可以力得也大賢學之
盡其力而造之難為功也其以是夫昔顏子自
言其學之所至意謂聖人之道雖高妙而難入
而其教我以博約也則有序而可循是以沉潜
于日用之間但覺其旨趣之深長也雖欲自已
不可得而已焉體驗于行事之際但見其意味
之真切也雖欲自止不可得而止焉鈎深致遠
而致其博者無一理之不窮則已罄吾智之所
===
能矣克己反躬而歸之約者無一事之不盡則
已殫吾力之所至矣於是向之所謂高者始得
以見其大原如有象焉卓然而立乎吾前也向
之所謂妙者乃得以識其定體若有形焉卓然
而在乎吾目也當斯時也於斯境也將勇往以
從之則幾非在我愈親而愈莫能即又何所施
其功乎將畢力以赴之則化不可為愈近而愈
莫能達又何所容其力乎顏子之自言如此可

The great worthy delighted in the profundity of the sage’s Way and exerted himself to the utmost; he perceived its true goal, yet found it difficult to make further progress. For the Way can be sought through effort, but cannot be attained through effort alone. Was this perhaps why the great worthy exhausted his strength in learning it, yet found it difficult to advance toward its attainment?

Long ago, when Master Yan spoke of the point his learning had reached, his meaning was this: “Although the sage’s Way is lofty and subtle, and difficult to enter, his teaching leads me through broad learning and disciplined restraint in an orderly sequence that I can follow. Thus, as I immerse myself in daily life, I feel only the profound and enduring significance of his teaching. Even if I wished to desist, I could not. As I test it in the conduct of affairs, I perceive only how true and immediate its meaning is. Even if I wished to stop, I could not. In plumbing the depths and reaching toward the distant to extend my learning broadly, I leave no principle unexplored: I have exhausted all that my understanding can accomplish. In mastering myself and examining my own conduct to return to disciplined restraint, I leave no matter unfulfilled: I have expended all the strength I possess.

“Only then do I begin to discern the great source of what I formerly called lofty, as though it had an image, standing towering before me. Only then do I come to recognize the constant substance of what I formerly called subtle, as though it had a form, rising distinctly before my eyes. At this time, in this state, if I would advance boldly to follow it, the incipient impulse is beyond my control: the more intimately I know it, the less I can draw up to it. Where, then, can I apply my efforts? If I would devote all my strength to reaching it, transformation cannot be forced: the nearer I come, the less I can attain it. Where, then, is there scope for my strength?”

Such was Master Yan’s account of himself. May he not be called one who deeply understood the sage and knew well how to learn from him? Nevertheless, what Master Yan referred to as…

末由者，豈真是而遂已哉？據其所已然，養其所未然，優柔厭飫，至于日深月熟而化焉，則亦將有不期而自至者矣。其終不克至是，而與聖人未達一間者，乃命焉，非學之過也。後之君子，尚無以其至之難而自沮也哉！

translation_en:
…when he spoke of having no way to proceed, could Yan Hui truly have stopped there? Building upon what he had already attained and nurturing what he had yet to attain, he could dwell at ease in his learning and steep himself fully in it, until, with daily deepening and monthly maturation, transformation occurred. Then something would come of itself, without being anticipated. That he ultimately failed to reach this point and remained one interval short of the sage was a matter of fate, not a fault in his learning. May gentlemen of later ages not let the difficulty of attaining it discourage them!
“When one knows how to cultivate oneself, one knows how to govern others; when one knows how to govern others, one knows how to govern the world, states, and families. There are nine constant principles for governing the world, states, and families: cultivating oneself, honoring the worthy, cherishing one’s kin, respecting great ministers, showing consideration for all officials, treating the common people as one’s children, attracting artisans of every kind, treating people from afar with kindness, and cherishing the feudal lords.”
Wang Xiangao 王顯高

是有關繫文字
考試官大學士李批長題須如此作方好
中庸論脩身之理於政之施者無不該舉為政
之經自身而推者有其序甚矣身之不可不脩
也中庸於此舉政以該於身而自身以推於政
也獨無意乎子思引孔子答哀公問政之言及
此謂夫為政固在於脩身吾身之理即在人之
理也誠知所以脩身則德立道行其於人也特

國家者乎身之可以該乎政者如此然天下國
家不可以徒治其政之經常者則有九焉夫惟

身之道當資於人故人之賢者必尊之而不敢
慢道之所進莫先其家故族之親者必親之而
不敢疎由家以及朝廷大小之臣皆立於朝者

中庸論脩身之理，於政之施者無不該舉；為政之經，自身而推者有其序。甚矣，身之不可不脩也！中庸於此舉政以該於身，而自身以推於政也，獨無意乎？子思引孔子答哀公問政之言及此，謂夫為政固在於脩身，吾身之理即在人之理也。誠知所以脩身，則德立道行，其於人也特推而及之耳，豈不知所以治人者乎？一人之理即眾人之理也。既知所以治人，則篤近舉遠，其於眾人也特舉而措之耳，豈不知所以治天下國家者乎？身之可以該乎政者如此。然天下國家不可以徒治，其政之經常者則有九焉。夫惟天下國家之本在身，故所謂脩身者其始也。脩身之道當資於人，故人之賢者必尊之而不敢慢；道之所進莫先其家，故族之親者必親之而不敢疎。由家以及朝廷，大小之臣皆立於朝者

Examiner Cheng, Academician, comments: By grounding the argument in self-cultivation, the diction becomes all the more refined and elegant. This is writing of consequence.

Examiner Li, Grand Secretary, comments: An extended topic must be treated in this way to be well handled.

The Doctrine of the Mean discusses the principles of self-cultivation, comprehensively embracing their application in government; the cardinal principles of governing, extended outward from oneself, have their proper sequence. How indispensable it is to cultivate oneself! Here the Doctrine of the Mean brings government within the compass of the self, then extends outward from the self to government. Could this be without purpose? Zisi quotes Confucius’s reply to Duke Ai’s question about government down to this point, meaning that governing indeed rests upon self-cultivation. The principles inherent in my own person are precisely those inherent in other people. If one truly understands how to cultivate oneself, virtue is established and the Way is put into practice. As regards others, one need only extend these to them. How, then, could one fail to understand how to govern others? The principles inherent in one person are precisely those inherent in the multitude. Once one understands how to govern others, one treats those nearby with generous care and brings those far away within one’s reach; as regards the multitude, one need only apply these principles to them. How, then, could one fail to understand how to govern the world, states, and families? Such is the way in which the self can encompass government. Yet the world, states, and families cannot be governed without means: there are nine constant principles of government. Since the foundation of the world, states, and families lies in the self, what is called self-cultivation comes first. The way of self-cultivation requires assistance from others; therefore one must honor the worthy and dare not slight them. In advancing the Way, nothing takes precedence over one’s own family; therefore one must cherish one’s kinsmen and dare not estrange them. Extending from the family to the court, ministers of greater and lesser rank are all those who serve at court …

也。於大臣則敬之而盡其禮，於群臣則體之而察其心。由朝廷以及其國，民工之衆皆聚於國者也。於庶民則子愛之以遂其生，於百工則招來之以盡其力。由其國以及天下，有遠人焉，則柔而服之，使之各得其所；有諸侯焉，則綏而懷之，使之不失其度。治天下國家之政，於是乎盡矣。政之自身而推者，又如此。然則人君豈可不以脩身為務哉？抑觀《中庸》之於九經，既起其端矣，下文乃歸之於誠。盖一有不誠，則九者皆虛文，而天下國家終不可得而治也。故又反之身焉，以極于學問思辨之事，言愈密而意愈至矣。子思是書，實亦萬世有天下國家者之法哉！

translation_en:
…so they are. He treats the great ministers with reverence, fully observing the rites due to them; he treats the other ministers with sympathetic understanding, discerning their hearts. Extending from the court to his state, the common people and artisans are all gathered within it. He loves the common people as his children, enabling them to sustain their lives; he attracts the various artisans, enabling them to exercise their abilities fully. Extending from his state to all under Heaven, he treats people from afar with kindness and wins their allegiance, allowing each to find a proper place; he brings peace to the feudal lords and wins their attachment, ensuring that they do not depart from their prescribed bounds. The measures for governing all under Heaven, the state, and the family are thereby complete. Such, too, is the way government extends outward from the person. How, then, could a ruler fail to make self-cultivation his principal concern? Consider further how the Doctrine of the Mean, having introduced the nine constant principles, subsequently grounds them in sincerity. For if sincerity is lacking in even one respect, all nine become empty formalities, and all under Heaven, the state, and the family can never be properly governed. Thus it returns once more to the person, carrying its discussion through to the tasks of learning, inquiry, reflection, and discrimination. Its words become ever more exact, and its meaning ever more complete. Truly, this book by Zisi is a model for those who possess all under Heaven, states, and families throughout the ages!
“The heart of compassion is benevolence; the heart of shame and aversion is righteousness; the heart of respect and reverence is propriety; the heart that distinguishes right from wrong is wisdom.”

不少貸者羞惡之心也是心也即性之義焉蓋
punctuated:
者鮮能體貼，類皆浮辭浪說。此篇辭不繁而理自足，盖得孟子之本旨者，是可錄也。
同考試官編修徐批：題本不難，求其認理真切、措辭穩帖如此篇者，盖亦鮮矣。
考試官學士程批：學者類能談性情，下手便錯。若此作，是誠有見者。
考試官大學士李批：說理文字，正不在多。
大賢因夫情之皆善，著其性之本然。盖情者心之用，而性則其體也。自非指其情之善而觀之，則性之善亦曷得而見哉？孟子因公都子疑性善之說而曉之者如此。且人之心，體用具焉。蘊而為仁義禮智之性，發而為惻隱羞惡恭敬是非之情者，皆同也。是故感阨窮之事而傷之切，念煢獨之人而痛之深者，惻隱之心也。是心也，即性之仁焉。盖仁之理主於愛，而所謂惻隱者皆愛也。使無是仁，則無是惻隱矣，而惻隱非仁乎？己有不善，愧耻而無所容；人有不善，憎疾而不少貸者，羞惡之心也。是心也，即性之義焉。盖
translation_en:
…few scholars can apprehend this personally; most offer only empty phrases and unrestrained talk. This essay is concise in expression yet fully adequate in principle. It grasps Mencius’s fundamental meaning and merits inclusion.
Associate Examiner Xu, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: The topic itself is not difficult, but essays that apprehend principle as truly and precisely, and express it as aptly and securely, as this one are indeed rare.
Examiner Cheng, a Hanlin Academician, comments: Scholars can generally talk about human nature and feelings, yet go wrong as soon as they begin. An essay such as this displays genuine insight.
Examiner Li, a Grand Secretary, comments: Writing that explains principle certainly does not depend on length.
The great worthy, drawing upon the goodness of all the feelings, revealed the original condition of human nature. Feelings are the functioning of the heart, while human nature is its substance. Unless one examines the goodness of the feelings, how can the goodness of human nature be seen? This is how Mencius enlightened Gongduzi when he doubted the teaching that human nature is good. Moreover, the human heart possesses both substance and function. What is stored within as the nature of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, and what issues forth as the feelings of compassion, shame and aversion, reverence and respect, and approval and disapproval, is common to all people. Thus, to be moved by circumstances of hardship and distress and feel keen sorrow, or to think of people who are alone and helpless and feel deep pain, is to possess the heart of compassion. This heart is precisely the benevolence of human nature. The principle of benevolence centers on love, and what is called compassion is entirely love. Without this benevolence, there would be no such compassion. Is compassion, then, not benevolence? When there is wrongdoing in oneself, to feel shame so keenly that one has nowhere to hide; when there is wrongdoing in others, to detest it and grant it not the slightest indulgence—this is the heart of shame and aversion. This heart is precisely the righteousness of human nature. For…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
義之理主於制而所謂羞惡者皆制也使無是
義則無是羞惡矣而羞惡非義乎至若容貌莊
肅於承接之時志意儼恪於對越之際者為恭
敬之心而禮之理實主於敬也茍無是禮則安
有所謂恭敬者乎是心也即性之禮也知人之
善而斷以為是知人之惡而别以為非者為是
非之心而智之理實主於别也茍無是智則安
有所謂是非者乎是心也即性之智也情之感
於物者隨所發而皆同性之具於心者本固有
===
而非外知情之皆善則性之本善可見矣抑前
篇言惻隱羞惡辭讓是非為仁義禮智之端而
此不言端者彼欲人擴而充之此直因用以著
其本體其意盖互相發耳孟子真知獨見擴前
聖所未發此說一行而諸家言性之失始破其
有功於斯道也不亦大乎
易
說以先民民忘其勞
楊廷儀

punctuated:
義之理主於制，而所謂羞惡者皆制也。使無是義，則無是羞惡矣，而羞惡非義乎？至若容貌莊肅於承接之時，志意儼恪於對越之際者，為恭敬之心，而禮之理實主於敬也。茍無是禮，則安有所謂恭敬者乎？是心也，即性之禮也。知人之善而斷以為是，知人之惡而别以為非者，為是非之心，而智之理實主於别也。茍無是智，則安有所謂是非者乎？是心也，即性之智也。情之感於物者，隨所發而皆同；性之具於心者，本固有而非外。知情之皆善，則性之本善可見矣。抑前篇言惻隱、羞惡、辭讓、是非為仁義禮智之端，而此不言端者，彼欲人擴而充之，此直因用以著其本體，其意盖互相發耳。孟子真知獨見，擴前聖所未發，此說一行，而諸家言性之失始破。其有功於斯道也，不亦大乎？

易
說以先民，民忘其勞。
楊廷儀
translation_en:
…the principle of righteousness centers on regulation, and what we call shame and aversion are both acts of regulation. Without this righteousness, there would be no such shame and aversion. Are shame and aversion, then, not righteousness itself? As for maintaining a solemn demeanor when receiving others and a reverent disposition when standing in the presence of the higher powers, these constitute the heart of respect and reverence. The principle of ritual propriety indeed centers on reverence. Without this ritual propriety, how could there be what we call respect and reverence? This heart is precisely the ritual propriety inherent in human nature. Recognizing goodness in others and judging it to be right, and recognizing evil in others and distinguishing it as wrong, constitute the heart of right and wrong. The principle of wisdom indeed centers on discrimination. Without this wisdom, how could there be what we call a sense of right and wrong? This heart is precisely the wisdom inherent in human nature. The feelings stirred by external things are common to all in each of their manifestations; the nature present in the heart is inherently possessed and does not come from outside. Once we understand that the feelings are all good, the original goodness of human nature becomes evident.

Moreover, the earlier chapter calls compassion, shame and aversion, deference and yielding, and the sense of right and wrong the beginnings of benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom. Here, however, it does not speak of beginnings. The earlier passage urges people to extend and fully develop them; this passage proceeds directly from their functioning to reveal their underlying substance. The meanings of the two passages thus illuminate one another. With true understanding and unique insight, Mengzi developed what the earlier sages had not yet articulated. Only when this teaching gained currency were the errors in the various schools’ accounts of human nature refuted. Was his contribution to this Way not indeed great?

Book of Changes
“Lead the people with joy, and the people forget their toil.”
Yang Tingyi

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
同考試官主事胡批平易說經而理致自
達其善於學易者歟
同考試官編修王批辭既切實理亦無遺
視彼專事浮豔者不侔矣
同考試官編修徐批題意明白作者猶或
紛紛拘泥者失之窘馳騁者失之泛平實簡當
不失為經學文字僅見此篇
考試官學士程批能發揮說之正處可取
考試官大學士李批形容得忘字最妙
===
惟上以說而率民則民亦說而趨事蓋勞非民
心之所說也今以說之道而率之則民之說而
忘其勞者殆有不期而然矣兌之彖傳釋卦辭
而極言說道之正先以順天應人於此則謂說
之為道所以感乎民者豈有所强而能哉其有
所先乎民者以佚而使之常必適其所欲無益
之工弗以勤也擇可而勞之不至乖其所願不
急之務弗以加也如播穀乘屋理不容於不為
則使之備所需以從事築城鑿池勢不可以但
punctuated:
同考試官主事胡批：平易說經，而理致自達，其善於學易者歟！
同考試官編修王批：辭既切實，理亦無遺，視彼專事浮豔者不侔矣。
同考試官編修徐批：題意明白，作者猶或紛紛，拘泥者失之窘，馳騁者失之泛。平實簡當，不失為經學文字，僅見此篇。
考試官學士程批：能發揮說之正處，可取。
考試官大學士李批：形容得忘字最妙。
惟上以說而率民，則民亦說而趨事。蓋勞非民心之所說也，今以說之道而率之，則民之說而忘其勞者，殆有不期而然矣。兌之彖傳釋卦辭，而極言說道之正，先以順天應人，於此則謂說之為道，所以感乎民者，豈有所强而能哉？其有所先乎民者，以佚而使之，常必適其所欲，無益之工弗以勤也；擇可而勞之，不至乖其所願，不急之務弗以加也。如播穀乘屋，理不容於不為，則使之備所需以從事；築城鑿池，勢不可以但
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Hu, Secretary: He expounds the classic plainly and clearly, and its principles emerge naturally. Surely he is skilled in studying the Book of Changes!
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Compiler: His language is pertinent and substantial, and his treatment leaves no principle unaddressed. He is quite unlike those who devote themselves exclusively to superficial ornament.
Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Compiler: The meaning of the topic is clear, yet writers still become entangled in it: those who cling rigidly to it err through constriction, while those who range freely err through diffuseness. For plainness, substance, concision, and aptness, while remaining a proper piece of classical scholarship, this essay alone stands out among those I have seen.
Comment by Examiner Cheng, Academician: He succeeds in elaborating what is correct in joy; this merits approval.
Comment by Examiner Li, Grand Secretary: His portrayal of the word “forget” is particularly fine.
When those above lead the people through joy, the people likewise undertake their tasks with joy. Toil is certainly not what delights the people's hearts. Yet if they are led by the way of joy, their delight and their forgetting of their toil will come about almost spontaneously, without being sought. The Commentary on the Judgments for Dui, Joy, explains the hexagram statement and fully expounds the correctness of the way of joy. It begins with following Heaven and responding to human beings; here it means that the way of joy moves the people—how could this be achieved through any compulsion? In taking the lead among the people, the ruler employs them with their ease in view, always ensuring that this accords with their desires, and does not toil them with useless projects. He chooses suitable tasks for their labor, ensuring that these do not run counter to their wishes, and does not burden them with affairs that are not urgent. For example, sowing grain and roofing houses are things that reason does not permit one to leave undone, so he has the people prepare what they need and set to work. As for building city walls and digging moats, circumstances do not permit simply…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
巳則使之執所業以赴工說以先民如此由是
民莫不曰田廬之利吾實資之以生容可緩乎
遠近奔走將不約而自同城池之設吾誠賴之
以安容可怠乎踴躍後先將不期而自集耕穫
經營勤則有矣而爭先于矻矻之際者未嘗以
為病巳焉版築疏鑿疲亦甚矣而効力于僕僕
之餘者未嘗以為厲巳焉吁上以說而率乎下
下以說而應乎上是上下皆一於正矣此說道
之所以為大歟大抵惡勞喜逸民之常也其有
===
所勞者豈聖人之得巳哉以其所說而勞之則
其勞也乃所以為逸也古先帝王惓惓愛養而
不忍傷民力者蓋以此耳後世託巡狩之名而
動眾于遊幸襲臺沼之迹而殫力于土木民勞
之詩作胥讒之念興夫豈獨下之罪哉為人上
者即彖傳之言而觀之可以鑒矣
過此以往未之或知也窮神知化德之盛
也
倫文叙

punctuated:
巳，則使之執所業以赴工。說以先民如此，由是民莫不曰：「田廬之利，吾實資之以生，容可緩乎？」遠近奔走，將不約而自同。「城池之設，吾誠賴之以安，容可怠乎？」踴躍後先，將不期而自集。耕穫經營，勤則有矣，而爭先于矻矻之際者，未嘗以為病巳焉；版築疏鑿，疲亦甚矣，而効力于僕僕之餘者，未嘗以為厲巳焉。吁！上以說而率乎下，下以說而應乎上，是上下皆一於正矣。此說道之所以為大歟！大抵惡勞喜逸，民之常也。其有所勞者，豈聖人之得巳哉？以其所說而勞之，則其勞也乃所以為逸也。古先帝王惓惓愛養而不忍傷民力者，蓋以此耳。後世託巡狩之名而動眾于遊幸，襲臺沼之迹而殫力于土木，《民勞》之詩作，胥讒之念興，夫豈獨下之罪哉？為人上者，即彖傳之言而觀之，可以鑒矣。
過此以往，未之或知也；窮神知化，德之盛也。
倫文叙
translation_en:
…be left undone, they are made to take up their respective tasks and proceed to the work. Such is leading the people through joy. Consequently, the people all say: “We truly depend on the benefits of fields and dwellings for our livelihood. Can we possibly delay?” From near and far they hurry forward, joining together without prior agreement. “We truly rely on the provision of city walls and moats for our security. Can we possibly be idle?” Eagerly pressing forward, one after another, they assemble without an appointed time. Plowing, harvesting, planning, and building certainly entail toil; yet those who vie to be first amid this strenuous labor never regard it as an affliction to themselves. Building with rammed earth, dredging, and excavating bring great exhaustion; yet those who continue exerting themselves after arduous effort never regard it as harm to themselves. Ah! Those above lead those below through joy, and those below respond to those above through joy: thus both above and below are united in what is right. Is this not what makes the way of joy so great?
Generally, disliking toil and enjoying ease are normal dispositions of the people. When the sage imposes labor on them, could he possibly avoid doing so? If he puts them to work on what gives them joy, their labor is precisely the means of securing their ease. Surely this alone explains why the emperors and kings of antiquity so solicitously cherished and nurtured the people, and could not bear to impair their strength. In later ages, rulers mobilized multitudes for pleasure excursions under the pretext of inspection tours, and exhausted the people's strength on construction projects in imitation of the terraces and pools of antiquity. The poem “The People Are Toiling” was composed, and thoughts of mutual slander arose. Could the fault lie solely with those below? Those who rule over others can find a warning by considering these words of the Commentary on the Judgments.
“Beyond this, none has yet known; to fathom the numinous and understand transformation is the fullness of virtue.”
Lun Wenxu

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
同考試官主事胡批此作庶幾洒然脫落
可與言神化矣
同考試官編修王批下學上達雖若相懸
而實相貫場中罕有得此意者發明精切無踰
此篇
同考試官編修徐批易為潔靜精微之書
而此題又易書之精者作此文字豈容雜以浮
辭辭愈多而去理愈遠矣此作就題說去而意
自了了豈皮膚臆見者所能道哉
===
考試官學士程批舉業于易者不及此
考試官大學士李批說理明盡結更有味
下學之上無可致之功上達之地有自致之妙
夫下學而上達自然之機也苟至於無所用カ
則亦何上達之不可致也哉且下學之事至於
精義利用而交養互發之機自不能已然義雖
極精猶在我也在精義以上則幾非在我矣用
雖極利猶有為也自利用以往則化不可為矣
欲擬議以求之而至理不容以頓悟已無念慮

同考試官編修王　批〔下學上達雖若相懸而實相貫場中罕有得此意者發明精切無踰此篇〕

考試官學士程　批〔學深于易者不及此〕
考試官大學士李　批〔說理明盡能更有味〕
===
下學之上無可致之功上達之地有自致之妙
夫下學而上達自然之機也蓋至於無所用力
則亦何上達之不可致也哉且下學之事至於
精義利用而交養互發之機自不能已然義雖
極精猶在我也自精義以上則幾非在我矣用
雖極利猶有為也自利用以往則化不可為矣
欲擬議以求之而至理不容以頓悟已無念慮
punctuated:
同考試官主事胡批：此作庶幾洒然脫落，可與言神化矣。
同考試官編修王批：下學上達，雖若相懸，而實相貫。場中罕有得此意者，發明精切，無踰此篇。
同考試官編修徐批：易為潔靜精微之書，而此題又易書之精者。作此文字，豈容雜以浮辭？辭愈多，而去理愈遠矣。此作就題說去，而意自了了，豈皮膚臆見者所能道哉？
考試官學士程批：舉業于易者不及此。
考試官大學士李批：說理明盡，結更有味。
下學之上，無可致之功；上達之地，有自致之妙。夫下學而上達，自然之機也。苟至於無所用カ，則亦何上達之不可致也哉？且下學之事，至於精義利用，而交養互發之機自不能已。然義雖極精，猶在我也；在精義以上，則幾非在我矣。用雖極利，猶有為也；自利用以往，則化不可為矣。欲擬議以求之，而至理不容以頓悟，已無念慮
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Hu, a Secretary, comments: This composition comes close to being serenely free of encumbrances. Its author is someone with whom one may discuss the numinous and transformation.
Associate Examiner Wang, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: Learning below and attaining understanding above may seem far apart, but in fact they are interconnected. Few in the examination hall have grasped this meaning. For precise and penetrating elucidation, no composition surpasses this one.
Associate Examiner Xu, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: The Book of Changes is a book of purity, stillness, subtlety, and profundity, and this topic concerns what is most profound within it. How could an essay on it admit a mixture of empty phrases? The more such words there are, the farther one departs from principle. This composition proceeds directly from the topic, and its meaning is clear of itself. How could anyone with merely superficial, conjectural views express such things?
Examiner Cheng, a Hanlin Academician, comments: Those who study the Book of Changes for the examinations do not reach this level.
Examiner Li, a Grand Secretary, comments: The exposition of principle is clear and exhaustive; the conclusion is still more rewarding.
Beyond learning below, there is no effort by which attainment can be secured; in the realm of understanding above, there is the subtle wonder of attainment coming of itself. For learning below and thereby attaining understanding above is a natural working. If one reaches the point where there is no occasion to exert effort [?], what higher understanding could remain unattainable? Moreover, when the work of learning below reaches the refinement of meaning and its beneficial application, the process by which these nourish and bring forth one another cannot cease of itself. Yet however refined meaning becomes, it still lies within oneself; beyond the refinement of meaning, the incipient workings are no longer within oneself. However beneficial the application becomes, it still involves deliberate action; beyond beneficial application, transformation cannot be brought about through deliberate action. One wishes to seek it through deliberation, yet ultimate principle does not permit sudden apprehension; already there are no thoughts or reflections …

translation_en:
…to which thought can be applied; who knows how to employ the mind here? One wishes to strive diligently to follow it, yet the wondrous Way admits of no hastening of transformation. There is already no work upon which effort can be expended; who knows how to apply one's strength here? Such is the absence, beyond learning below, of any achievement attainable through effort. As for the numinous, it is the spiritual potency of Heaven and Earth, present in yin and in yang yet unfathomable; nevertheless, one can fully penetrate the subtle mystery of why it is so. Transformation is the Way of change in Heaven and Earth, becoming yin and becoming yang through gradual stages; nevertheless, one can understand the incipient workings by which it operates. By what action, then, is this actually attained? It is simply that virtue accumulated within becomes thoroughly integrated, pure, and mature, and forms a unity with the numinous: without one's awareness, they accord with one another. Virtue exalted within becomes full, abundant, and great, and forms a unity with transformation: without one's awareness, they flow through one another. Is this not the subtle efficacy by which attainment comes of itself in the realm of higher understanding?

Ah! What is not known is the going forth and contracting; what is attained of itself is the coming back and extending. This, too, is merely the natural principle of stimulus and response. What need is there for anxious, restless thought? Now, when our Master explained the words of the fourth, yang line of the hexagram Influence (Xian), he discussed the principles of the world as rooted in a single unity. From speaking of the principle of contraction and extension, going and coming, he extended his discussion to learning, which likewise has its own spontaneous workings. Only at this point does his explanation reach its fullest extent. For learning below and attaining understanding above are really not two separate matters. Between the absence of self-directed effort and numinous transformation [?], there is not room for a hair: precisely this is what learners find difficult. Certainly one must not force it through deliberate intention, nor may one forget it through inattention.

translation_en: …what one gains will be limited, with no ground for further accumulation, and one’s virtue will be narrow. Thus, wherever virtue is found, one must not cling to a single source as one’s teacher; goodness alone must be one’s guide. If goodness is here and I learn from it, the goodness here becomes my own; if goodness is there and I learn from it, the goodness there likewise becomes my own. Seeking on every side and gathering from afar, one hears of every good quality; storing and accepting them all, one acquires every good quality. In this way, one draws abundantly and broadly upon the principles embodied in others. When the principles of the world are viewed in reverse, from their myriad diverse manifestations, their fundamental source, comprehensively united within oneself, has never been other than one. If one gathers them without reducing them to their essentials, then, however much one acquires, they have no final resting place, and one’s goodness remains diffuse. Thus, wherever goodness is found, one must not cling to a single instance as one’s guide; only through unity can one bring it all into harmony. If one can harmonize good qualities, great and small alike, then the goodness in one’s own mind is all the goodness of the world. If one can harmonize good qualities, whether many or few, then the goodness of the world is precisely the goodness in one’s own mind. Bringing them together and embracing them all, one comprehends their full breadth, leaving nothing out; joining and thoroughly integrating them, one attains their utmost purity, without admixture. In this way, the principles within oneself are threaded together by a single unity and reduced to their essentials. Beginning by seeking principle in its myriad diverse manifestations and ending by apprehending its subtle workings in a single root: could anything remain undisclosed about the essentials of drawing on others to cultivate goodness? Indeed, these words of Yi Yin set out the sequence of learning to become a sage. While living in retirement, he recited the Odes and read the Documents, delighted in the Way of Yao and Shun, and grasped the purport of refinement and single-mindedness. Upon entering public service, he used this understanding to assist Cheng Tang; both possessed a single virtue, and he brought to the utmost the work of extending beneficence…

…achievement. When he withdrew from office, he again used this teaching to admonish Tai Jia. His resolve to make his ruler a Yao or Shun and his people like theirs never changed with retirement or service, old age or youthful vigor. Tai Jia observed Yi Yin’s instructions and was able to perfect his virtue to the end, becoming an excellent king of Shang. Is this not also an example that rulers through all ages ought to follow?
“Let the present king reflect: ‘The former kings diligently employed their illustrious virtue, winning allegiance and securing support. The many states presented offerings, and those treated as brothers came from every quarter: this too resulted from employing illustrious virtue. The kings thus presided over and assembled the many states, which presented abundant offerings. August Heaven entrusted the people of the central lands and their territories to the former kings. Therefore, let the king employ virtue to bring harmony and joy to the misguided people, guiding and assisting them, and thereby bring joy to the former kings who received Heaven’s mandate. Having taken this as his mirror, let him desire that it extend to ten thousand years, and that the king’s sons and grandsons forever protect the people.’”
Bian Yi.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Supervising Secretary: It explains emulating the virtue of former kings and seeking an enduring mandate. Its meaning has lasting resonance. An excellent composition.
Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Compiler: It successfully conveys the idea that a ruler employs virtue to bring glory to his predecessors and provide abundantly for his successors. The conclusion returns the emphasis to the people, making it still more pointed and admonitory.
Comment by Associate Examiner Fei, Admonisher: It is not difficult to produce an essay on a long topic, but most submissions are tiresomely confused and disordered. Those that strive for brevity, meanwhile, simply omit words from the topic altogether. This essay alone strikes the proper balance between fullness and concision. It is an outstanding exposition of the meaning of the Classics.

Examiner Li, Grand Secretary, comments: The prose brims with energy, yet contains not a single superfluous phrase. Here precisely lies the difficulty; readers should appreciate it for themselves.

When a great minister admonishes his ruler, he wishes him both to carry forward his predecessors’ virtue so as to transform all under Heaven and to transmit the royal enterprise so as to preserve all under Heaven. For the predecessors’ virtue is the foundation of the royal enterprise. If one understands how to transform all under Heaven, the means of preserving it lie therein. In former times, a great minister of Zhou offered admonition to his ruler, speaking as follows: The realm today is the realm of the former kings. Can our king fail to consider how to carry on the work of his predecessors? Thus the greatly illustrious King Wen won the allegiance of the feudal lords in the days when he exercised independent authority to conduct punitive expeditions. He worked diligently and thoroughly to spread his luminous virtue far and wide. Even the distant Jiang and Han regions he nurtured as though they were the western lands. Thus, when the many states presented their offerings, they were as close as brothers, coming from every quarter; they too all employed luminous virtue to set an example for those below. King Wu, who grandly continued this legacy, won the allegiance of the feudal lords after conquering Shang. He worked diligently and thoroughly to extend his luminous virtue everywhere. Even the distant Cai and Wei domains he governed as though they lay within the royal domain. Thus, when the many states presented their offerings, they were as harmonious as elder and younger brothers, arriving from every quarter; they too all employed luminous virtue to provide a model for those below. The king should follow the old statutes to bring harmony and concord to the many states, ensuring not merely that those nearby are obedient, but also that those far away are won over and come to him. Then royal standards will not be debased, and ever more feudal lords will come to present their offerings. title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
綏之責至大也中國之疆土文武既受之皇天
奄甸之寄至重也王當用明德以作新迷民不
惟和悅之有方而且勞來之無倦則邦本以固
而先王之受命者可慰矣所謂繼先德以化天
下者如此然陳戒之辭雖終而祈君之意無已
也吾王可不思所以監於此乎是故用德以化
諸侯者欲由是而垂裕後昆必我周之國統可
至於萬年用德以化迷民者欲由是而啟佑後
人必我周之國祚可延於萬世繼王之身有子
===
焉子而又子永保乎庶邦之民萬年如一日也
繼王之子有孫焉孫而又孫永保乎中國之民
萬世如一時也所謂傳王業以保天下者又如
此大臣之忠愛其君也一何至哉大抵有天下
者莫先於得天天之所輔則王業可永然視聽
好惡天未嘗不因乎人焉故有周大臣言祈天

編斷簡亦不外是周過其歷固以此也後之君
臣尚亦知所監哉

punctuated: 綏之責至大也。中國之疆土，文武既受之皇天，奄甸之寄至重也。王當用明德以作新迷民，不惟和悅之有方，而且勞來之無倦，則邦本以固，而先王之受命者可慰矣。所謂繼先德以化天下者如此。然陳戒之辭雖終，而祈君之意無已也。吾王可不思所以監於此乎？是故用德以化諸侯者，欲由是而垂裕後昆，必我周之國統可至於萬年；用德以化迷民者，欲由是而啟佑後人，必我周之國祚可延於萬世。繼王之身有子焉，子而又子，永保乎庶邦之民，萬年如一日也；繼王之子有孫焉，孫而又孫，永保乎中國之民，萬世如一時也。所謂傳王業以保天下者又如此。大臣之忠愛其君也，一何至哉！大抵有天下者，莫先於得天，天之所輔，則王業可永。然視聽好惡，天未嘗不因乎人焉。故有周大臣言祈天，必歸諸用德；言用德，必歸諸保民。雖間見於殘編斷簡，亦不外是。周過其歷，固以此也。後之君臣，尚亦知所監哉！
translation_en:
…the responsibility for bringing them peace is immense. As for the territory of the Central States, Kings Wen and Wu received it from August Heaven; the charge of governing it in its entirety is exceedingly weighty. The king should employ luminous virtue to renew the misguided people. He must not only have the means to bring them harmony and contentment, but also be tireless in comforting and drawing them to him. Then the foundation of the state will be secure, and the former kings, who received the Mandate, may be consoled. Such is what is meant by carrying on the virtue of one’s predecessors to transform all under Heaven.

Yet although the words of admonition have ended, the hopes placed in the ruler have no end. Can our king fail to consider how to take this as his example? Thus, employing virtue to transform the feudal lords is intended to leave abundant blessings to later descendants, ensuring that the dynastic succession of our Zhou may last ten thousand years. Employing virtue to transform the misguided people is intended to guide and aid those who come afterward, ensuring that the dynastic fortune of our Zhou may endure for ten thousand generations. After the king himself come his sons, and after sons, further sons, forever protecting the people of the many states, through ten thousand years as through a single day. After the king’s sons come his grandsons, and after grandsons, further grandsons, forever protecting the people of the Central States, through ten thousand generations as through a single moment. Such, in turn, is what is meant by transmitting the royal enterprise to preserve all under Heaven. How consummate is a great minister’s loyalty and love toward his ruler!

In general, for one who possesses all under Heaven, nothing takes precedence over winning Heaven’s favor. If Heaven lends its aid, the royal enterprise can endure forever. Yet in seeing and hearing, loving and hating, Heaven invariably follows the people. Thus, when the great ministers of Zhou spoke of seeking Heaven’s favor, they invariably referred the matter back to the practice of virtue; when they spoke of practicing virtue, they invariably referred it back to protecting the people. Though their words appear only here and there in fragmentary texts and broken slips, they never depart from this principle. It was indeed for this reason that Zhou outlasted its allotted span. May the rulers and ministers of later ages also know what to take as their example!

Yao Ting

Comment by Associate Examiner Shao, a bureau director: “The final two lines of this stanza express a hope. Candidates in the examination generally expounded them as an actual event. This essay conveys the poet’s intent, and so it has been selected.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Jia, a compiler: “Its account of the spirit in which the people of Wei delighted in goodness at that time stirs the reader to emulation. This is what is valuable in the poem’s moral influence.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Pu, a compiler: “It gives an almost complete expression to the poet’s subtle and gently indirect meaning. Here is someone with whom one may discuss poetry.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Gu, a compiler: “The admirable way in which the grandee set aside his rank and humbled himself before a worthy man is indeed apparent in his carriages, horses, and banners. Yet it is wrong to say that these things alone constituted respect. Writers attend closely to each phrase, but risk fragmenting the text [?]; and in discussing ‘what words will he offer him,’ they often mix in stale expressions, departing far from the poet’s intent. text:
也其意深夫尊賢下士大夫之盛節也詩人樂
道其事而望賢者有以告之其深有所感乎昔
衞大夫見賢者於下邑其國人相聚而竦觀於
是作詩以道其事至此謂夫我大夫之来也建
其旌焉則孑孑干旟特出於浚城属以素絲實
羽儀之至美也乗其車焉則良馬騑騑並列於
驂服至於六轡蓋禮秩之加盛也羽儀之美不
自以為尊而躬造夫賢者之廬禮秩之盛不知
其為貴而親致夫下士之舉大夫於此其亦可

translation_en:
…the sentiment is profound. Honoring the worthy and humbling oneself before men of learning are eminent virtues in a great officer. The poet delights in recounting this deed and hopes that the worthy man will have something to tell him. Must he not have been deeply moved?

Formerly, a great officer of Wei visited a worthy man in an outlying town. The people of the state gathered to watch with reverent attention, and a poem was composed to recount the event. At this point it says: when our great officer arrives and raises his banner, the lofty banner with its tortoise-and-snake and bird designs [?] stands prominently above the walls of Jun. Fastened with white silk cords, it displays the utmost beauty of ceremonial adornment. When he rides in his carriage, fine horses move in stately procession, the outer and central horses arrayed together, with six reins: the ceremonial distinctions of rank are all the more splendid. Yet despite the beauty of his ceremonial display, he does not consider himself exalted, but goes in person to the worthy man's humble dwelling. Despite the splendor of his ceremonial rank, he is unmindful of his high station and personally humbles himself before a man of learning. In this, the great officer may indeed be called diligent!

That gentleman lives in seclusion to pursue his aspirations; never before has he heard a summons accompanied by jade and silk. This is truly a splendid undertaking. What, one wonders, will he actually say during their meeting to reciprocate the respect first shown to him? He has nurtured his virtue and awaited the proper time, never taking part in the governance of noble households or states. Now indeed is his time. What instruction, one wonders, will he give when consulted, to reciprocate the sincerity of this visit? Will he speak? We cannot know; his accumulated resources for ordering affairs are surely beyond the discernment of those of shallow understanding. Will he remain silent? We cannot know; plans for the court are likewise no concern of people on the roadside. Ah! Is this why the poet expresses his hopes so deeply and cannot refrain from speaking?

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
以為作於衞文公之世今不可考也而先儒謂
衞國之禍本以二詩之所刺者致之文公中興

translation_en:
…takes it to have been composed in the time of Duke Wen of Wei; this can no longer be verified. Earlier Confucian scholars held that Wei’s calamities had their origins in the conduct condemned by the two poems. Duke Wen’s restoration was precisely a time of taking warning from past events and fostering the beginnings of goodness; hence the poem took this form. Although the events concerned a single state, a great warning for all the world and all succeeding ages is plainly manifest here. When it is said that the Poems can be used to observe, surely this is the sort of thing meant!
“The crossboards and uprights are set in place; on the raised teeth, feathers are planted. The ying and tian drums [?], the suspended drums, the pellet drums, chime stones, and wooden zhu and yu instruments—once all are ready, the music begins, with panpipes and pipes sounding together.”
Zhang Tianxiang

Comment by Associate Examiner Pu, Hanlin Editor: “He unfolds an account of the music of the Zhou dynasty, with its sequence and organization perfectly ordered.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Gu, Hanlin Editor: “Those who compose expositions of the Eulogies of Zhou often merely enumerate the names of things. If that were truly enough, what need would there be for literary composition? An essay such as this, which brings richness out of dry material, certainly makes the examining officials [?] regard it with fresh eyes.”
Comment by Examiner Cheng, Academician: “At any rate, this is a piece with which the author himself feels well pleased.”

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
考試官大學士李批文字中亦有始終條理
章
樂之陳也具器飾之美樂之作也極小大之全
夫樂有器有飾而其大與小各有所用也陳之
而具其美作之而極其全周家一代之樂盛矣
哉吾想周之盛時功成治定禮既制矣樂亦作
焉於是合之袒廟之中新夫一王之制其所以
縣夫樂者有業虞焉設業以附栒而植虞於栒
端戴璧垂羽而鼓磬於是乎縣也所以為縣之
===

搖有鞀垂擊有磬傍列柷敔而始終之節皆有

translation_en:
Examiner, Grand Secretary Li, comments: “The writing, too, displays orderly arrangement from beginning to end.”

Section

When the musical ensemble is arrayed, it possesses the full beauty of instruments and ornaments; when the music is performed, it achieves completeness in both small and great. Music has its instruments and ornaments, and the great and small each have their uses. Arrayed, they display all their beauty; performed, they realize their full completeness. How magnificent was the music of the Zhou dynasty!

I imagine the flourishing age of Zhou: achievements accomplished and government settled, ritual had been instituted and music was also created. Then the ensemble was brought together within the ancestral temple [?], inaugurating the institutions of a new royal order. For suspending the musical instruments, there were ornamental boards and uprights [?]. The boards were fitted to the crossbars, and the uprights stood at the crossbars’ ends, bearing jade discs and hanging feathers; from this framework the drums and chime stones were suspended. For decorating the suspension frame, there were projecting teeth. These were fashioned upon the crossbars and ornamental boards, and birds’ feathers were set upright to give a stately appearance. Colors were applied to depict things, completing the decorative patterns.

The small drum was the ying, and the large drum the tian. They were hung from the crossbars and uprights, and at this point the institutions of Xia and Shang underwent a transformation. There were handled rattle drums to shake and suspended chime stones to strike; beside them stood the wooden chu percussion box and yu scraper, providing all the instruments needed to mark the beginning and ending of the music. Yet could this have been merely a matter of having everything in place?

Then the music cleansed and stirred, displaying the accomplished achievements of the dynasty. Rattle drums and drums sounded together, and panpipes made of assembled bamboo joined in. The many tones combined into an ordered composition; clear and deep tones brought one another out, each realizing the utmost subtlety of its sound. The music subdued and uplifted, representing the flourishing virtue of the former kings. Bronze bells and stone chimes sounded harmoniously, while pipes blown together entered at intervals. Thus the many musicians assembled and performed together, the high…

text:

有如是夫抑周樂之見於詩者多矣皆因事而

translation_en:
…the low notes respond to the high, each fully realizing the principle of mutual resonance and communication. Ah! Such was the splendor of the music made by the people of Zhou! Moreover, Zhou music appears frequently in the Odes, but elsewhere it is mentioned in connection with particular events. This poem alone concerns its first performance, with the ensemble playing together in the ancestral temple; hence its account of the music is especially detailed. Its descriptions of the crossbars and uprights of the instrument racks, their projecting teeth, and the rattle drums, chime stones, panpipes, and pipes also illuminate, and are illuminated by, the Book of Yu and the Rites of Zhou. Does not the Record of Rites say: “Those whose government is well ordered have complete rites; those whose achievements are great have fully developed music”? The magnificent virtue and great accomplishments of Kings Wen and Wu and the Duke of Zhou can thus be adequately discerned in this poem.

Spring and Autumn Annals

“The feudal lords covenanted at Kuiqiu”—the ninth year of Duke Xi. “They joined in a covenant at Pingqiu”—the thirteenth year of Duke Zhao.

Qin Li

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Vice Director: The merits and faults of Qi and Jin involve many strands, which generally leave writers at a loss. This paper reduces complexity to simplicity while clearly leaving out none of the relevant events or principles. It comes close to attaining the concise and lucid method of the Spring and Autumn Annals.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Hanlin Compiler: On this topic concerning the covenant assemblies of Dukes Huan and Zhao, the narratives in most papers are tiresomely tangled. This essay embeds approval and censure within its exposition and stands out for its clarity and order. It deserves inclusion among the selected papers.

Comment by Examiner Cheng, Academician: The passage explaining the five prohibitions and the five improprieties is brilliant…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
可為作義者法
考試官大學士李批經義中亦有辭之複而
不厭者此類是也
信講而備禁之美者可予信講而備事之惡者
可譏此齊桓之盟葵丘晉昭之盟平丘春秋皆
以複辭書之而二伯之美惡判矣且葵丘曷為
而盟邪齊桓主伯欲修舊好嘗偕六國之君以
會於此公以諸侯雖輯而王禁不可不明也於
是束牲免歃血之禮載書致申命之辭而葵丘
===
之盟講焉是盟也君子以為美蓋初命所中凡
以脩身正家也而任賢之道再命以之三命所
申凡以字民柔遠也而官人之道四命以之至
若篤邦交而守臣度則又命之五也自春秋以
來為盟者眾矣未有美之備若此盟者是可以
常辭書哉故會盟同地而再書葵丘書之重辭
之複見其為美之大而予之也若平丘又曷為
而盟邪晉昭嗣伯欲討携貳嘗徵十有二國之
君以會於此公以諸侯有間而伯威不可不示

可為作義者法。
考試官大學士李批：經義中亦有辭之複而不厭者，此類是也。
信講而備禁之美者可予，信講而備事之惡者可譏。此齊桓之盟葵丘、晉昭之盟平丘，《春秋》皆以複辭書之，而二伯之美惡判矣。且葵丘曷為而盟邪？齊桓主伯，欲修舊好，嘗偕六國之君以會於此。公以諸侯雖輯，而王禁不可不明也，於是束牲，免歃血之禮；載書，致申命之辭，而葵丘之盟講焉。是盟也，君子以為美。蓋初命所中，凡以脩身正家也；而任賢之道，再命以之；三命所申，凡以字民柔遠也；而官人之道，四命以之；至若篤邦交而守臣度，則又命之五也。自《春秋》以來，為盟者眾矣，未有美之備若此盟者，是可以常辭書哉？故會盟同地，而再書葵丘。書之重，辭之複，見其為美之大而予之也。若平丘，又曷為而盟邪？晉昭嗣伯，欲討携貳，嘗徵十有二國之君以會於此。公以諸侯有間，而伯威不可不示
translation_en:
…may serve as a model for those composing essays on the meaning of the Classics.
Examiner, Grand Secretary Li, comments: Even in essays on the meaning of the Classics, there are instances in which repeated wording does not weary the reader. This is one such instance.
When good faith is affirmed [?] and the prohibitions are comprehensively set forth, the merit deserves approval; when good faith is affirmed [?] but the conduct is thoroughly evil, it deserves censure. Thus, in recording Duke Huan of Qi’s covenant at Kuiqiu and Duke Zhao of Jin’s covenant at Pingqiu, the Spring and Autumn Annals uses repeated wording in both cases, yet clearly distinguishes the merit and wrongdoing of the two hegemons.
Why, then, was the covenant at Kuiqiu concluded? Duke Huan of Qi, presiding as hegemon and wishing to renew old friendships, had assembled there with the rulers of six states. The duke considered that, although the feudal lords were united, the royal prohibitions still had to be made clear. He therefore had the sacrificial animal bound but dispensed with the rite of smearing blood upon the lips; in the covenant document he set forth words reiterating the injunctions. Thus the covenant at Kuiqiu was established.
The gentleman regards this covenant as admirable. What the first injunction addressed [?] concerned cultivating oneself and ordering one’s household. The second injunction concerned the way to employ worthy men. What the third injunction reiterated concerned nurturing the people and conciliating those far away. The fourth concerned the way to appoint men to office. As for strengthening relations between states and observing the proper bounds of a subject’s conduct, these formed the fifth injunction. Throughout the period covered by the Spring and Autumn Annals, many covenants were concluded, but none possessed such complete excellence as this one. Could it therefore be recorded in ordinary language? Thus, although the meeting and the covenant took place at the same location, Kuiqiu is written twice. The repeated recording and repeated wording reveal the greatness of its merit and express approval of it.
As for Pingqiu, why was its covenant concluded? Duke Zhao of Jin, succeeding to the hegemony and wishing to punish those who had become estranged or divided in their allegiance, had summoned the rulers of twelve states to assemble there. The duke considered that there were divisions among the feudal lords and that the hegemon’s might had to be displayed…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
也於是耀之以辛未之兵恐之以壬申之斾而
平丘之盟同焉是盟也君子以為惡蓋劉獻公
天子之老瀆之以同歃一惡也楚棄疾夷狄之
賊懼之而結盟又一惡焉矜兵甲之威以脅齊
一惡也信蠻夷之訴以絕魯又一惡焉至若以
威詐涖盟而無禮義忠信之心則又惡之一也
自春秋以来同盟者衆矣未有惡之備若此盟
者亦豈可以常辭書哉故會盟同地而再書平
丘書之重辭之複見其為惡之大而譏之也噫

則知昭伯之所以衰聖人一予之一譏之辭不
嫌於同而義各有所當矣雖然晉昭不足道也
齊桓初命不免躬自犯之況震矜一萌而叛者
九國其賢於晉昭者無幾矣顧功以桓公為首
盟以葵丘為最春秋之所美者豈聖人之得已

也。於是耀之以辛未之兵，恐之以壬申之斾，而平丘之盟同焉。是盟也，君子以為惡。蓋劉獻公，天子之老，瀆之以同歃，一惡也；楚棄疾，夷狄之賊，懼之而結盟，又一惡焉。矜兵甲之威以脅齊，一惡也；信蠻夷之訴以絕魯，又一惡焉。至若以威詐涖盟，而無禮義忠信之心，則又惡之一也。自春秋以来，同盟者衆矣，未有惡之備若此盟者，亦豈可以常辭書哉？故會盟同地而再書平丘，書之重、辭之複，見其為惡之大而譏之也。噫！觀葵丘之盟，則知桓伯之所以盛；觀平丘之盟，則知昭伯之所以衰。聖人一予之，一譏之，辭不嫌於同，而義各有所當矣。雖然，晉昭不足道也，齊桓初命不免躬自犯之，況震矜一萌而叛者九國，其賢於晉昭者無幾矣。顧功以桓公為首，盟以葵丘為最，春秋之所美者，豈聖人之得已哉？故世之言治者，當以王道為正，無徒曰齊桓云爾。

齊人侵我西鄙，公追齊師至酅，弗及。〔僖公〕
translation_en:
… was necessary. Accordingly, he displayed his troops to them on the xinwei day and intimidated them with his banners on the renshen day, and so they joined together in the covenant at Pingqiu. The gentleman regards this covenant as evil. Duke Xian of Liu was a senior servant of the Son of Heaven: to dishonor him by making him join in the blood oath was one evil. Qiji of Chu was a villain among the barbarians: to conclude a covenant out of fear of him was another evil. To flaunt military might in order to intimidate Qi was one evil; to believe the accusations of the barbarians and exclude Lu was another. To preside over the covenant through intimidation and deceit, without any concern for ritual propriety, righteousness, loyalty, or trustworthiness, was yet another evil. Since the beginning of the Spring and Autumn period, many have joined in covenants, but none has encompassed evils so completely as this one. How, then, could it be recorded in ordinary language? Thus, although the meeting and covenant took place at the same location, Pingqiu is named twice. The repeated recording and wording reveal the magnitude of its evil and condemn it.

Alas! By examining the covenant at Kuiqiu, one understands why Duke Huan’s hegemony flourished; by examining the covenant at Pingqiu, one understands why Duke Zhao’s hegemony declined. The Sage approves the one and condemns the other. He does not avoid using the same wording, yet its meaning is appropriate to each case. Nevertheless, Duke Zhao of Jin hardly merits discussion, while even Duke Huan of Qi could not avoid personally violating the first injunction of his covenant. Moreover, as soon as arrogance and intimidation arose in him, nine states rebelled. He was scarcely better than Duke Zhao of Jin. Yet in achievements Duke Huan ranks first, and among covenants Kuiqiu ranks highest. Could the Sage have done otherwise than praise these in the Spring and Autumn Annals? Therefore, those in this world who discuss government should take the Kingly Way as their standard, rather than merely speak of Duke Huan of Qi.

The men of Qi invaded our western borderlands. The duke pursued the army of Qi as far as Xi but did not catch up with it. 〔Duke Xi〕…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
二十六年
林庭㭿
同考試官員外郎趙批齊魯用兵之失見
於經傳甚明作者往往斷非其罪且以為易而
忽之歟此作體認親切而文足以發之蓋邃於
經學者
同考試官編修吳批融會胡傳意責齊魯
私憤用兵詞鋒森然可謂健筆
考試官學士程批得旨
===
考試官大學士李批寫交罪二國意極明切
内外以憤而用兵也皆失其正春秋隨事而立
文也交致其譏此西鄙之侵其罪在齊而至巂
之追其罪在魯也觀聖人之書法可見矣且齊
魯之為釁也始於無虧之救重以洮向之盟於
是齊孝憤魯窺西鄙以見侵魯僖憤齊追至巂
而弗及春秋何以交致其譏邪蓋自齊觀之罪
魯而討其瀆盟若有辭矣聖人則曰彼盟自瀆
我何與焉縱欲討之威以文告使之自曲而請

punctuated:
二十六年。
林庭㭿。
同考試官員外郎趙批：齊魯用兵之失，見於經傳甚明。作者往往斷非其罪，且以為易而忽之歟？此作體認親切，而文足以發之，蓋邃於經學者。
