考試官學士程批：得旨。
考試官大學士李批：寫交罪二國意，極明切。
内外以憤而用兵也，皆失其正；春秋隨事而立文也，交致其譏。此西鄙之侵，其罪在齊；而至巂之追，其罪在魯也。觀聖人之書法可見矣。且齊魯之為釁也，始於無虧之救，重以洮向之盟。於是齊孝憤魯，窺西鄙以見侵；魯僖憤齊，追至巂而弗及。春秋何以交致其譏邪？蓋自齊觀之，罪魯而討其瀆盟，若有辭矣。聖人則曰：彼盟自瀆，我何與焉？縱欲討之，威以文告，使之自曲而請
translation_en:
…the twenty-sixth year.
Lin Tingang 林庭㭿.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Vice Director: The faults in Qi’s and Lu’s use of troops are very clearly shown in the Classic and its commentaries. Writers often condemn them for offenses other than those they actually committed. Can it be that they consider the subject easy and therefore treat it carelessly? This composition grasps the meaning closely and precisely, and its prose adequately brings that understanding out. Its author is evidently deeply versed in classical scholarship.
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Compiler: Integrating the meaning of Hu’s Commentary, this essay censures Qi and Lu for deploying troops out of private resentment. Its language has a formidable edge: this may well be called vigorous writing.
Comment by Examiner Cheng, Academician: It captures the essential meaning.
Comment by Examiner Li, Grand Secretary: It expresses with great clarity and precision the intention to condemn both states.
Both the home state and the outside state deployed troops out of resentment, and both departed from what was right. The Spring and Autumn Annals frames its wording according to the circumstances and directs its censure at both. For this invasion of the western borderlands, the fault lay with Qi; for the pursuit as far as Xi, the fault lay with Lu. This is apparent from the Sage’s manner of recording the events. Now the hostility between Qi and Lu began with the intervention to aid Wukui and was aggravated by the covenants at Tao and Xiang. Duke Xiao of Qi, resentful of Lu, watched for an opportunity on its western frontier and invaded; Duke Xi of Lu, resentful of Qi, pursued its troops as far as Xi but failed to overtake them. Why does the Spring and Autumn Annals censure both? From Qi’s perspective, it seemingly had grounds to condemn Lu and punish it for violating the covenant. But the Sage says: “Their violation of that covenant was their own doing. What had I to do with it? Even if one wished to punish them, one should overawe them with a written proclamation, causing them to acknowledge their own fault and request…”

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
服善也今以潜師掩魯人之不備而掠其西鄙
示之弱以相誘伏其衆以求逞襲盜賊之謀報
睚眦之憾何名乎是故書侵以見其潜入書人
書師以見其有所誘而徼其利也然則齊人之
兵以私憤興焉而非正也明矣自魯觀之追齊
而因其來侵似無過矣聖人則曰彼理自屈我
何校焉苟欲卻之諭以辭命使之不縮而引去
善也今以孤軍乗齊師之既歸而直造敵境信
其弱以窮追見彼強而遽返蹈不測之險犯否
臧之戒何義乎是故書追至酅以見其深入書
弗及以見其有所畏而不敢遂也然則魯之兵
以私憤應焉而非正也又明矣吁一書法之間
而二罪皆不可掩聖人之言不亦簡而盡乎抑
考前此魯嘗敗齊而桓公屈己以平之遂成一
匡之業者管仲之力也後此北鄙見伐而魯人
陳先王之盟言齊遂引去者展禽之策也使孝
公得如管仲者相之而展禽見用於僖公則所
謂私憤之兵孰從而致乎此為國者在於任賢

punctuated: 服，善也。今以潜師掩魯人之不備，而掠其西鄙，示之弱以相誘，伏其衆以求逞，襲盜賊之謀，報睚眦之憾，何名乎？是故書「侵」以見其潜入，書「人」、書「師」以見其有所誘而徼其利也。然則齊人之兵以私憤興焉而非正也，明矣。自魯觀之，追齊而因其來侵，似無過矣。聖人則曰：「彼理自屈，我何校焉？苟欲卻之，諭以辭命，使之不縮而引去，善也。」今以孤軍乗齊師之既歸，而直造敵境，信其弱以窮追，見彼強而遽返，蹈不測之險，犯否臧之戒，何義乎？是故書「追至酅」以見其深入，書「弗及」以見其有所畏而不敢遂也。然則魯之兵以私憤應焉而非正也，又明矣。吁！一書法之間，而二罪皆不可掩，聖人之言不亦簡而盡乎？抑考前此，魯嘗敗齊，而桓公屈己以平之，遂成一匡之業者，管仲之力也。後此北鄙見伐，而魯人陳先王之盟言，齊遂引去者，展禽之策也。使孝公得如管仲者相之，而展禽見用於僖公，則所謂私憤之兵孰從而致乎？此為國者在於任賢
translation_en:
…submit: that would have been good. Instead, they secretly advanced their army, caught the people of Lu unprepared, and plundered their western borderlands. They feigned weakness to lure them on and concealed their troops in ambush to secure their ends, adopting the schemes of robbers to avenge a petty grudge. What justification could there be for this? Thus, the text writes “invaded” to reveal their stealthy entry, and uses the designations “men” and “army” to reveal that they were laying a lure and seeking advantage from it. It is therefore clear that Qi’s military action arose from private resentment and was not righteous.

From Lu’s perspective, pursuing Qi in response to its invasion might seem faultless. But the Sage says: “They themselves are in the wrong; why should we contend with them? If we wish to repel them, we should admonish them through diplomatic communications and cause them to withdraw without yielding [?]: that would be good.” Instead, with an isolated force, they took advantage of the Qi army’s withdrawal to advance directly into enemy territory. Believing Qi weak, they pursued it to the utmost; seeing its strength, they abruptly turned back. They ventured into unforeseeable danger and violated the warning against an ill-considered undertaking. What righteousness could there be in this? Thus, the text writes “pursued as far as Xi” to reveal how deeply they penetrated, and “did not catch up” to reveal that they were afraid and dared not continue. It is therefore also clear that Lu’s military response arose from private resentment and was not righteous.

Ah! Within a single instance of the annalistic method, neither offense can be concealed. Are the Sage’s words not both concise and comprehensive? Consider, moreover, what happened before this: Lu once defeated Qi, but Duke Huan humbled himself to make peace with Lu and ultimately accomplished the task of setting the realm in order. This was due to Guan Zhong’s efforts. Later, when Lu’s northern borderlands were attacked, the people of Lu set forth the words of the covenant made by the former kings, whereupon Qi withdrew. This was Zhan Qin’s strategy. Had Duke Xiao obtained someone like Guan Zhong to serve as his chief minister, and had Zhan Qin been employed by Duke Xi, how could such military actions born of private resentment have arisen? Thus, governing a state depends upon employing the worthy…

translation_en:
…and military force cannot be relied upon. This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals gives the matter such profound and unremitting attention.

Record of Rites

“When instruction at the Great Learning begins, vegetable offerings are presented while wearing the leather cap, to demonstrate reverence for the Way. The first three odes of the Minor Odes are rehearsed, to give students an initial grounding for official service. Upon entering the school, the drum is sounded and the book boxes opened, to instill submission to their studies. The two implements, the catalpa rod and the thorn switch, are used to maintain proper awe. Before the date of the di sacrifice has been determined by divination, there is no inspection of the school, allowing students’ aspirations free scope. They are observed from time to time without being told what to do, so that they preserve their attentiveness. Younger students listen without asking questions: learning must not skip stages.”

Bi Zhao

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Chief Supervising Secretary: “The exposition of a long topic should be concise and clear. Straying into verbosity and obscurity is a common failing among examination candidates. This essay merits inclusion.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Hanlin Academy Compiler: “The main purport of this topic from the Record of Learning is clear, but its many strands make an orderly, polished treatment difficult. This essay weaves material from the Collected Explanations into a coherent composition, concise without being obscure. Its conclusion especially brings out the completeness of the ancients’ methods of instruction. It deserves to be selected for inclusion.”

Comment by Examiner Cheng, Academician: “The subtlety of those passages where its reasoning is refined and orderly cannot be appreciated without close reading.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Grand Secretary: “Reading this exposition, one scarcely notices how many strands the topic contains. This is indeed an accomplished writer.”

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
記者歷序大學之事而各著其所教之義焉蓋
士非教不成也然則大學教之之事何莫而不
有其義哉且古之王者建國君民必先教學而
其所以為教者其義何在邪彼學者入學之初
有司衣皮弁之服潔蘋藻之常儀而舉夫先師
之祭者所以示尊敬道藝之誠而端其趨向也

translation_en:
The compiler recounts in sequence the affairs of the Great Learning and sets forth the purpose of the instruction embodied in each. Scholars cannot become accomplished without instruction; what practice of instruction in the Great Learning, then, could fail to have its purpose? Moreover, the kings of antiquity, when establishing states and ruling the people, invariably gave priority to teaching and learning. What purposes underlay their methods of instruction?

When students first entered the school, the responsible officials donned robes with leather caps, performed the customary rites with purified aquatic plants, and offered sacrifice to the former teachers. This demonstrated sincerity in revering the Way and the arts, and set the students’ aspirations in the right direction. At the vegetable offering, they sang the three poems from the Lesser Odes and practised their words of feasting and rewarding service. This showed the honor of holding office and accepting responsibility, and encouraged their initial aspirations. Upon entry into the school, the Senior Music Instructor beat the drum to summon the students, and they opened their book chests and took out their texts. They were thereby made to cultivate humility and obedience, free of arrogance and indolence, so that their studies might advance.

Once the students had entered the school, the responsible officials fashioned rods of catalpa and thornwood for punishment and made the school’s disciplinary penalties clear to warn against indolence. This made the students compose their bearing and guard against idle and improper conduct, so that their learning would not lapse. That the ruler did not inspect the school and assess the scholars before the time for divining the date of the di sacrifice was no matter of laxity: it allowed the students to proceed at ease and bring their aspirations to fulfillment. That, during the inspection, instruction was not given by explaining everything in full was no matter of concealment: it was intended to have the students silently apprehend what they learned and retain it in their minds.

As for the younger students, they might not yet be able to ask questions; even if they could, they might not know what was essential. Thus they merely listened to and received their teachers’ explanations without asking questions. Was this not because the sequence of advancement in learning and cultivation must not be confused, and the gradations between elder and younger must not be overstepped? Ah! Wherever a practice was carried out, there was…

punctuated:
一事之教，此古者大學之法所以為至歟！抑不特此也，其時教則有正業，其退息則有居學，其考校則自一年以至九年，皆有所視焉。盖其為脩齊治平之業者，無一而不豫養之也。等而上之，則有能食之教，有能言之教，至於八歲而有小學之教，所以培養之而為大學之根本者密矣。宜其化行俗美，而非後世之所及也哉！

樂者敦和，率神而從天；禮者别宜，居鬼而從地。故聖人作樂以應天，制禮以配地。

王守仁

同考試官都給事中林批：「近時經生率以此禮樂為造化自然，恐但云禮樂便渉制作上說。不然，則敦和别宜，造化豈自敦且别邪？此作是也。」

同考試官修撰劉批：「作此題者多體認欠明，徒務敷演，浮冗可厭，盖時習之弊也。是卷說理措辭，精深典雅，而其氣充然，豈拘拘摹倣之士哉！」
translation_en:
…instruction for each undertaking: is this not why the ancient system of higher learning attained such perfection? Yet it was not limited to this. Its seasonal instruction had a prescribed curriculum; its periods of rest and leisure had learning to be pursued outside formal lessons; and its assessments, from the first year through the ninth, each examined particular attainments. In all the endeavors of cultivating oneself, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the realm, there was nothing for which it did not nurture the foundations in advance. Tracing the stages back further, there was instruction when children could eat, instruction when they could speak, and, at eight years of age, instruction in elementary learning. How thorough was the nurture that established the foundations of higher learning! Little wonder that its transforming influence spread and its customs became excellent, beyond anything later ages could attain!

“Music fosters harmony, leads the spirits, and follows Heaven; ritual distinguishes what is fitting, gives the ghosts their proper places, and follows Earth. Thus the sages created music to respond to Heaven and established ritual to accord with Earth.”

Wang Shouren.

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Chief Supervising Secretary: “Nowadays students of the Classics generally take the ritual and music mentioned here to mean the spontaneous workings of creation, apparently fearing that merely speaking of ritual and music would bring the discussion into the realm of deliberate institution. But otherwise, in ‘fostering harmony’ and ‘distinguishing what is fitting,’ could creation itself do the fostering and distinguishing? This essay is correct.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Compiler: “Most who write on this topic lack clarity in their understanding and devote themselves merely to elaboration, producing tiresome superficiality and verbosity. This is indeed a fault of current practice. This paper is penetrating and profound in its exposition of principles, refined and elegant in its diction, and full of vigor. Could its author be a scholar confined to slavish imitation?”

Examiner Cheng, Academician, comments: In a discussion that probes the foundations, passages concerning the creative transformations of the cosmos are especially difficult to write. Works whose language and reasoning flow forth as abundantly as in this essay are rare indeed.

Examiner Li, Grand Secretary, comments: Fluent and lucid, without blemish. Among essays on the meaning of the Record of Music, this alone meets the standard.

Precisely because ritual and music accord with the subtle workings of cosmic creation and transformation, the sages accomplish their work of establishing institutions. Ritual and music indeed flow in mutual communication with cosmic transformation. Yet without the sages establishing them, how could the work of participating in and assisting that transformation be accomplished? And how, in fact, can we see that ritual and music accord with cosmic transformation?

Thus, the intermingling of cosmic forces transforms things into their fullest substance: this is the spontaneous harmony of cosmic transformation. It is the expansion of vital energy, qi, becoming spirit, shen—the means by which Heaven generates things. Music, in its functioning, takes harmony as its guiding principle. Through its unfolding and stirring movement, it deepens that harmony in the outward manifestations of nurturing life. Does it not follow the expansion of qi and thereby accord with Heaven? The high and the low are dispersed and differentiated: this is the spontaneous order of cosmic transformation. It is the contraction of qi, becoming ghost, gui—the means by which Earth brings things to completion. Ritual, in its functioning, takes order as its guiding principle. Through regulation, moderation, limitation, and restraint, it distinguishes what is appropriate amid the vast expanse of things. Does it not gather in the contracting qi and thereby accord with Earth?

Such is the accord of ritual and music with cosmic transformation. Thus, when sages arise, they follow its spontaneous harmony and create music. All the patterned arrangements of the five notes and six pitch standards—whether endings and beginnings generating one another, or high and low tones responding to one another—are grounded in this harmony. Could they be merely intended to delight the eye and ear? Through them the sages respond to the harmony of cosmic transformation, causing yang …

translation_en:
…from becoming excessively overbearing, so that their work of bringing things to life is one with Heaven’s. Following the natural order of creation, the sages established ritual. Its three thousand minor and three hundred major prescriptions—whether graded institutions or specified names and objects—all take that order as their model. Could these be merely instruments of embellishment? Through them the sages accord with the order of creation, preventing yin from becoming excessively severe, so that their work of bringing things to completion is inseparable from Earth’s. How great, then, is the achievement of the sages’ institutions, through which they participate in and assist the work of Heaven and Earth!

Yet let us examine this further. The Way of Heaven and Earth does not extend beyond yin and yang, and ghosts and spirits are the numinous powers of yin and yang. The Way of the sages does not extend beyond ritual and music, and harmony and order are the Way of ritual and music. In substance these are simply one; those who do not understand divide them into two. Thus, understanding why yin and yang, ritual and music, are one enables us to recognize the subtlety of the sages’ institutions. As for those who arrogate to themselves communication between Earth and Heaven and profane the distinction between the unseen and the visible realms, theirs are surely not what we mean by ghosts and spirits. What use, then, is what they call ritual and music?

…those who do understand are nevertheless constrained by their command of the brush and cannot fully express its meaning. Writing that expounds principles is most difficult. The arguments in this piece pour forth from the breast in an unbroken stream, seemingly without deliberate effort. Moreover, its understanding of principle is subtle and profound, its language full and substantial, free of the habits and mannerisms currently in vogue. I believe that through this I can discern what you have cultivated within yourself.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Hanlin Academy Compiler: There are certainly many fine pieces in the discourse section. Yet although on first reading they seem delightfully eloquent and wide-ranging, closer scrutiny reveals that they all discuss acting according to the Mean as circumstances require; none addresses the topic precisely. This too results from prevailing fashions. The chief examiners did not choose the topic without a purpose. Then I obtained this paper, which thoroughly discusses the meaning of standing in the center without leaning to either side. Every stage of its argument has a clear origin and development, and all its emphases and qualifications remain within the topic. Its author is evidently deeply versed in the learning of human nature and principle. Judging from this, is it only in your writing that you remain unaffected by prevailing fashions?

Comment by Examiner Cheng, Hanlin Academician: Among the compositions in the discourse section, the expansive ones mostly err in being weak, while the concise ones err in being obscure. None had fully satisfied me. Suddenly I came upon this paper. Its verbal force is like water surging and mountains rising, with meaning and principle moving along with it. It has rises and falls, and it reaches a proper conclusion. Where fullness is called for, it is vigorous; where brevity is called for, it is clear. Reading it, I feared only that it would end. title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
向也如是以往亦將何所底極乎此篇見理真
切措詞條暢亦何嘗無開合起伏於其間而終
不出乎繩準之外為論學者可以觀矣
獨立乎道之中而力足以守之非君子之勇不
能也蓋中固難於立尤難乎其守也中立而有
以守之必其識足以擇理而不惑於他岐行足
以蹈道而不陷於僻地力足以勝私而不誘於
外物天下之事紛紜轇轕乎吾前而吾之中固
在也使徒立之而力不足以守之則執於此或
===
移於彼植於前或仆於後矜持於旦夕無事之
時而顛蹶於倉卒不備之際向之所謂中立不
旋踵而已失之矣此中立而不倚者所以見君
子之强而為天下之大勇歟且君子之所以自
立者何中而已是道也原於帝降著於民彝其
體本不倚也然一事有一事之中一時有一時
之中有定理而無定在焉今夫人之所自立也
譬之地焉高者或亢遠者或曠皆過乎中卑者
或汙近者或局皆不及乎中是蓋擇之不精而

translation_en:
…sounds [?]. If this continues, to what extreme will it ultimately lead? This essay apprehends principle truly and precisely, and its language is orderly and fluent. It certainly has its openings and closings, its rises and falls, yet it never departs from the proper standards. Those learning to compose discourses may take it as an example.
To stand alone in the mean of the Way, with strength sufficient to hold to it, is impossible without the courage of the gentleman. For while taking one’s stand in the mean is certainly difficult, holding to it is harder still. To stand in the mean and be able to maintain it requires discernment sufficient to choose what accords with principle without being confused by other paths, conduct sufficient to tread the Way without straying into deviant ground, and strength sufficient to overcome selfishness without being enticed by external things. Though the affairs of the world crowd before me in tangled confusion, my mean remains secure. If one merely takes one’s stand there but lacks the strength to maintain it, then what one holds to here may shift elsewhere; what stands firm at first may later fall. One may maintain a careful bearing in the uneventful course of daily life, yet stumble when sudden events catch one unprepared. What was formerly called standing in the mean will then be lost before one can turn on one’s heel. Is this not why standing in the mean without leaning to either side manifests the gentleman’s strength and constitutes the greatest courage under Heaven?
Moreover, by what does the gentleman establish himself? By the mean alone. This Way originates in what the Lord on High has bestowed and is manifest in the enduring moral norms of the people; in its essential constitution, it has no inclination to either side. Yet each affair has its own mean, and each moment has its own mean: there is a constant principle, but no fixed position. Now, the positions in which people establish themselves may be compared to terrain. What is high may be excessively elevated; what is distant may be too remote: both go beyond the mean. text:

中之體省察之精有以達乎中之用故能事事
而擇之時時而處之履道於至正之區而特立
乎流俗之外置身於至當之地而標見乎衆目
之表自卑者視之以為太高而不知其高之為
中也自高者視之以為太卑而不知其卑之為
中也以至于近遠亦然當出而出當處而處出
處之立乎中也當辭而辭當受而受辭受之立
乎中也以至于動靜語黙皆然然則君子之立

然則君子之立也，可謂中矣，又何以見其不倚邪？譬之物焉，有所憑則易以立，無所恃則易以倚。吾之所立者中，則或前或後，無可恃之人；或左或右，無可憑之物。以外誘言之，則聲色之私有以眩吾中，貨利之私有以撼吾中。苟吾之力不足以勝之，其不至於顛仆者寡矣。以已私言之，則辨或倚於私辨而非中，智或倚於私智而非中。苟吾之力不足以自勝，其不至於攲側者亦寡矣。故中立固難，立而不倚尤難。君子則以一定之守，持一
translation_en:
…their ability to hold firm is scarcely worth discussing. The gentleman, however, through mature cultivation and nurture of his moral nature, can establish himself in the substance of the mean; through meticulous scrutiny of himself, he can fully realize the mean in practice. Thus, in every affair he can choose it, and at every moment situate himself within it. He treads the Way in the realm of utmost rectitude, standing independently beyond prevailing customs; he places himself where it is most fitting, standing conspicuously before all eyes. Those who take a low position regard him as too high, without understanding that his height constitutes the mean; those who take a high position regard him as too low, without understanding that his lowliness constitutes the mean. The same applies to nearness and distance. He enters public service when he ought to enter it and remains in retirement when he ought to remain there: in service and retirement he stands in the mean. He declines when he ought to decline and accepts when he ought to accept: in declining and accepting he stands in the mean. The same applies to activity and stillness, speech and silence.
If the gentleman’s stance may thus be called the mean, how, further, can we see that he does not lean to either side? Consider physical objects: with something to lean against, they stand easily; without support, they easily tilt. If the position in which I stand is the mean, then neither before nor behind me is there anyone on whom I can rely; neither to my left nor to my right is there anything against which I can lean. As for external temptations, selfish desires for sensual pleasures can bewilder my sense of the mean, and selfish desires for wealth and profit can shake it. If my strength is insufficient to overcome them, rarely will I avoid falling. As for one’s own selfishness, argument may lean toward self-serving argument rather than the mean, and intelligence may lean toward self-serving cleverness rather than the mean. If my strength is insufficient to overcome myself, rarely, too, will I avoid tilting to one side. Thus, standing in the mean is indeed difficult; standing without leaning is more difficult still. text:
定之見不必有所憑也而確乎有不可拔之勢
不必有所恃也而屹乎有不可動之力激之而
不能使之高抑之而不能使之卑前之而不能
引後之而不能掣聲色自美耳吾之中終不為
其所眩貨利自靡耳吾之中終不為其所撼辨
有所不當施則不倚於辨智有所不當用則不
倚於智於所當處也雖迫之使出而有所不從
於所當辭也雖强之使受而有所不屑以至于

國有道無道而不變為君子之强蓋所謂中庸
之不可能者孔子因子路問强而告之所以抑
其血氣之剛而進之以德義之勇也彼子路者

…a settled conviction. He need not have anything to lean upon, yet stands firm with a strength that cannot be uprooted; he need not have anything to rely upon, yet stands lofty with a power that cannot be moved. Stir him up, and he cannot be made to rise; press him down, and he cannot be made to sink. Lead him forward, and he cannot be drawn along; pull him backward, and he cannot be dragged away. Sensual pleasures may have their own beauty, yet my inner balance will never be dazzled by them; wealth and profit may have their own allure, yet my inner balance will never be shaken by them. Where disputation ought not to be employed, I do not lean upon disputation; where cleverness ought not to be used, I do not lean upon cleverness. Where I ought to remain, even if pressed to leave, there are demands I will not obey; where I ought to decline, even if compelled to accept, there are things I disdain to take. This holds true of all affairs under Heaven. Though the affairs of the world differ in countless ways, the position on which I stand has never been lost. Thus, although he lives among other people, what he steadfastly maintains truly surpasses them. What courage under Heaven could exceed this?
Viewed in this light, wisdom is that by which one chooses; benevolence is that by which one acts; courage is that by which one holds fast. Courage brings wisdom and benevolence to completion and enables one to attain the mean. Yet a distinction must also be made: the strength of the south falls short of the mean, while the strength of the north goes beyond it. Only being harmonious without drifting with the current, standing in the mean without leaning to either side, and remaining unchanged whether the state possesses the Way or not constitute the strength of the gentleman. This is what is meant by the difficulty of practicing the constant mean. When Zilu asked about strength, Kongzi instructed him in this, seeking to restrain the toughness of his physical temper and advance him toward the courage of virtue and righteousness. translation_en:
…Your sagely gifts are Heaven-bestowed. Brilliant and outstanding, you emulate the admirable example of the founding ancestor; reverent, frugal, compassionate, and humane, you embody the excellent instructions of the Grand Empress Dowager. At this time of reforming government and retuning its strings, all eyes have newly turned toward you in eager expectation. The return of a venerable elder has stirred the court, while banishment to the maritime frontier has recalled the exile of the Sanmiao. As you approach the prime of life, your inquiry and learning should advance daily.

〔Your servant Zuyu〕 early attained examination honors and undeservedly took a place among the officials. In ten years at the historiographical bureau, I rendered no worthy service in compilation; in five years at the imperial lectures, I received successive promotions, reaching the office of Remonstrance Officer. Reflecting that I have failed to contribute even a drop of water or a speck of dust, I feel shame at wearing the insignia and ribbons of office. I consider that □ one can find a teacher for oneself [?]; even the greatest sage must still study. I have examined the records preserved in earlier writings and consulted the statutes and institutions of our dynasty. Tracing their origins, I begin with Paoxi; surveying their culmination, I extend to your late imperial father. The teachings of the mind transmitted and received throughout this period, together with the surviving words of lectures and explanations—all that concerns the work of rectifying oneself and cultivating virtue—I have compiled and set forth, extending even to enlightening people and bringing affairs to completion…

translation_en:
…as for these profound principles, I have investigated their origins in full and recorded them together in a single work, divided into eight juan and expressly entitled Learning for Emperors (Dixue), for Your Majesty’s august consideration. Yet, in searching through passages and selecting phrases, I have been unable to glimpse the subtleties of higher understanding. Nevertheless, establishing the fundamental substance and putting it into practice have already produced demonstrable results. Recorded on bamboo and silk, these may be verified for a hundred generations; applied to the state, they bring orderly government to the myriad lands. I dare not compare this work with the admonitions of the Cinnabar Writing (Danshu), but hope it may serve the purpose of the Admonition on the Great Treasure (Dabao).
I humbly wish that Your Majesty might keep it at hand in moments of leisure and graciously read and reflect upon it each day. Do not regard the worthies of the past as too remote, nor rest content with the modest achievements of recent times. To extend the Great Way, take the Three Sovereigns as your models; to consider consummate virtue, examine the Five Emperors. Follow the pattern of the achievements bequeathed by the Three Dynasties, and emulate the grand designs of successive sage rulers. In respectfully receiving instruction, emulate the worthiness of Qi of Xia; in humility of mind, continue the excellence of the Shang king Gaozong. You will surely add brilliance to the sun and moon, spreading their illumination without limit; matching Heaven and Earth in virtue, you will establish lasting peace and tranquillity.

…they are often unfamiliar with the institutions and precedents of our dynasty. Although their energies are limited, their understanding also falls short. This essay can recite the books in which our Sagely Progenitor left his instructions and give a full account of them. Its language is classical and its meaning dignified: surely its author is a man of discernment!
Examiner and Grand Secretary Li comments: Strengthening the foundations and fostering harmony among imperial kinsmen are indeed the deepest aims of the Sagely Son of Heaven in seeking good government, inherited from his imperial ancestor. This policy essay succeeds in celebrating and supporting them. To be loyal, a subject must first possess a sense of duty that makes him care for the state as for his own family. With a man such as this, one may indeed discuss loyalty.
Sagely government begins in the family, providing a standard for its application to the state; sagely instructions draw upon the past, providing rules to be handed down to posterity. This is why our Emperor Taizu composed the two books, Ancestral Instructions (Zuxun) and Record of the Clear Mirror (Zhaojian lu). How great are these imperial words! Born too late, I, in my ignorance, have had no opportunity to examine the holdings of the imperial repository. Yet through what fathers and teachers have transmitted and scholar-officials have related, I have heard of a work called Record of Sagely Government (Shengzheng ji), and have grasped its essentials. 東宮、親王，慮俗儒之是古非今、姦吏之舞文弄法，以妄動成訓，刊梓以藏，世守弗墜。又命儒臣編輯歷代諸王善可為法、惡可為戒者，為《昭鑒錄》，以賜諸王，令王府官僚進讀，以資日益。所以重根本以定人心，蕃枝葉以為屏衛。蓋凡聖政之在天下者，本末兼該，巨細畢具，而此其先也。
竊嘗因是而考之：堯之睦族，舜之徽典，夏有典則，殷有冊典，至周尤備。漢文帝因鼂錯之言，以法術賜太子，命賈誼以《詩》《書》教梁王。唐太宗作《帝範》以賜太子，而飭躬闡政之道明；玄宗作《開元訓》以示諸王，而父子君臣之義顯；作詩六章，札於步障，以賜太子，而仁孝之理彰。宋太宗出《戒子篇》，令郭贄講說以諭諸王，而為善去惡之
translation_en:
…the Crown Prince and the imperial princes. Concerned that commonplace scholars might uphold antiquity while condemning the present, and that unscrupulous officials might manipulate legal wording and twist the laws, thereby recklessly altering the established instructions, he had them printed from woodblocks and preserved, to be upheld through the generations without falling into neglect. He also commanded Confucian officials to compile examples of princes of successive dynasties whose good conduct could serve as a model and whose evil conduct could serve as a warning, making these into the Record of the Clear Mirror (Zhaojian lu). He bestowed it upon the princes and ordered the officials of their princely establishments to read it aloud to them, to aid their daily improvement. These measures strengthened the roots so as to settle the people's hearts and fostered the branches and leaves so that they might serve as a protective screen. The sage's governance of the realm encompassed both roots and ramifications and provided for everything great and small; yet this was its foremost concern.
I have ventured to examine earlier precedents in light of this. Yao brought harmony to his kin, and Shun established splendid norms; the Xia had canonical rules, and the Yin had written canons. By the Zhou these provisions were especially complete. Emperor Wen of the Han, acting on Chao Cuo's advice, bestowed writings on laws and administrative techniques upon the Crown Prince and commanded Jia Yi to instruct the Prince of Liang through the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents. Emperor Taizong of the Tang composed the Model for Emperors (Difan) and bestowed it upon the Crown Prince, thus making clear the way to discipline oneself and develop good government. Emperor Xuanzong composed the Instructions of the Kaiyuan Reign (Kaiyuan xun) to show the princes, thereby making manifest the proper relations between father and son and between ruler and minister. He composed six poems and inscribed them upon a screen, which he bestowed upon the Crown Prince, thus illuminating the principles of benevolence and filial piety. Emperor Taizong of the Song issued the Admonition to Sons (Jiezi pian) and ordered Guo Zhi to expound it to instruct the princes, thereby providing a mirror for doing good and abandoning evil…

…the lessons became manifest. Zhenzong assembled the imperial clansmen and bestowed upon the crown prince the Account of the Heir Apparent (Yuanliang shu), thereby spreading the influence of the four arts and the three virtues. He compiled the Essential Outline for the Heir Apparent (Chenghua yaolüe), thereby expanding discussion of succeeding to the throne and governing the people. Although these writings varied in depth, and their accounts in detail, their purpose was one: to instruct the heir apparent and admonish the branches of the imperial lineage.
We reverently reflect that when His Majesty the sagely Son of Heaven succeeded to the precious throne, his first act was to establish the imperial heir. Separate appointments were made for his guardians and preceptors, and Confucian officials delivered lectures. Everything they taught comprised the essential principles of the sages and worthies; everything they presented comprised the established precedents of emperors and kings. Following the old institutions, His Majesty then enfeoffed princes with their domains, assigning posts for their guidance and officials for their instruction. These arrangements both awakened their good hearts and nurtured constancy in their dispositions. All such measures had been practiced in high antiquity, yet were beyond the attainments of the intervening ages. Today the heir to the throne possesses discerning wisdom, and those of the imperial surname widely exhibit sincere familial harmony. The virtuous disposition of King Cheng assuredly sufficed to secure the peace of the Zhou house; the rites and music cultivated by the prince of Hejian likewise sufficed to contribute to the flourishing of the Han house. Yet preserving prosperity and maintaining inherited achievements have been considered difficult since antiquity; the effects of one's station on one's bearing and of nurture on one's physique likewise call for habitual care. title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
燕閒之際取是書而陳之因言析理必證以
典謨隨地獻忠必質諸行事
作聖之功務有臻于實效勸忠之誼不徒事
乎虛文俾知
櫛風沐雨之勞則所以守之者不容於不謹
知
分茅胙土之重則所以保之者不容於不至
聖祖在天之靈於是乎可慰而
國家億萬載隆長之業端在是矣請以是為
===
職輔導列王官者告焉謹對
第二問
倫文叙
同考試官主事胡批學以識洽辭為難此
篇洞悉言外而具得其要領殆胸中有經濟者
同考試官編修王批此卷學博識精才充
氣偉而紀綱風俗一策則援古證今鑿鑿可施
於時三復之餘竦然起敬噫天下士如是者可
多得邪

第二問
同考試官主事胡
倫文叙
批〔學以議治體為難此篇洞悉古今而且得其要領殆胸中有經濟者〕
同考試官編修王
批〔此卷學博識精才充氣偉而紀綱風俗一策則援古證今鑿鑿可施於時三復之餘竦然起敬噫天下士如是者可多得耶〕
punctuated:
燕閒之際，取是書而陳之，因言析理，必證以典謨；隨地獻忠，必質諸行事。作聖之功，務有臻于實效；勸忠之誼，不徒事乎虛文。俾知櫛風沐雨之勞，則所以守之者不容於不謹；知分茅胙土之重，則所以保之者不容於不至。聖祖在天之靈於是乎可慰，而國家億萬載隆長之業端在是矣。請以是為職輔導列王官者告焉。謹對。

第二問

倫文叙

同考試官主事胡批：學以識洽辭為難，此篇洞悉言外，而具得其要領，殆胸中有經濟者。

同考試官編修王批：此卷學博識精，才充氣偉，而紀綱風俗一策，則援古證今，鑿鑿可施於時。三復之餘，竦然起敬。噫！天下士如是者，可多得邪？
translation_en:
…during moments of leisure, take up this book and present it for consideration. In explaining its words and analyzing their principles, invariably adduce evidence from the Canons and Counsels; in offering loyal advice as circumstances arise, invariably test it against actual deeds. Efforts to cultivate sagehood must attain practical results, and the duty of encouraging loyalty must not be discharged through empty formalities alone. Let them understand the toil of being combed by the wind and bathed by the rain, so that they cannot but exercise care in preserving their inheritance. Let them understand the gravity of receiving sacrificial thatch and grants of territory, so that they cannot but do their utmost to safeguard them. Thus may the spirit of the Sagely Founder in Heaven be comforted. Here indeed lies the foundation for the state's flourishing and enduring enterprise through countless ages. I ask that this be conveyed to the officials charged with guiding and instructing the princes. Respectfully submitted in reply.

Second Question

Lun Wenxu

Comment by Associate Examiner Hu, Bureau Secretary: In learning, breadth of understanding and command of expression are difficult to attain [?]. This essay fully grasps what lies beyond the words and comprehends all the essential points. Its author surely possesses the capacity for ordering the affairs of the realm.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Compiler: This examination script displays broad learning, penetrating understanding, abundant talent, and magnificent spirit. The policy essay on governing order and social customs draws on antiquity to substantiate its arguments about the present; its proposals are well grounded and can be implemented in our own time. After reading it repeatedly, I was moved to profound respect. Ah! Can many scholars such as this be found in the world?

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
同考試官編修徐批前場得之知為佳士
及觀五策尤卓偉不羣其於
聖製儒學治體時務皆歷歷精究發之筆下沛然有餘今所録者
雖其一二然即是以求亦自異於人人矣
考試官學士程批五策皆有識見而發于
詞者舂容典實畧無衒露非積學氣充者不能
有此也觀者得其一固可以占其餘乎
考試官大學士李批此卷初場詞理俱到論

以化乎上皆世之所繫以為安危治亂者
也上不統乎下則名分陵夷而治之體不
立下不化乎上則習尚頹靡而治之用不
行然必上有所統而後下有所化故紀綱
之立實風俗之所由成也善言治者惡可
以為汎常闊遠而不加之意哉且所謂紀

Upon reading his five policy essays, I found him still more outstanding and extraordinary. Imperial compositions, Confucian learning, the principles of government, and current affairs—all have been clearly and thoroughly investigated, and flow abundantly from his brush. Although only one or two of his pieces are recorded here, even these suffice to show that he stands apart from ordinary men.”

Examiner Cheng, a Hanlin Academician, comments: “All five policy essays display discernment. Their expression is measured, elegant, and substantial, without the slightest ostentation. Examiner Li, a Grand Secretary, comments: “In this script, both expression and reasoning in the first session are fully accomplished, and the discourse matches them. The five policy essays are especially magnificent, revealing a brilliant spirit within their harmonious refinement. Such attainment requires accumulated learning and sustained cultivation. His elevation to first place among the many candidates gives us cause for mutual congratulation. The policy essay on institutional discipline and social customs is exceptionally sound in its arguments, and has therefore been specially recorded.”

Institutional discipline is the means by which those above govern those below; social customs are the means by which those below are transformed by those above. The security or peril, order or disorder of the age depend upon both. If those above do not govern those below, distinctions of status deteriorate and the framework of government cannot be established. If those below are not transformed by those above, prevailing habits decline and the practical work of government cannot proceed. Yet those above must exercise governance before those below can undergo transformation. Thus the establishment of institutional discipline is truly the foundation upon which social customs are formed. title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
綱風俗者上古之時無有也自五子之歌
陶唐是載棫樸之詠文王是歌而紀綱之
名始立書之風動見于虞典易之善俗繋
於周象而風俗之名始著盖綱猶網之有
綱紀猶絲之有紀綱其大也紀其小也上
行下效謂之風衆心安定謂之俗民函五
常之性剛柔緩急音聲不同繋水土之風
氣者風也好惡取舍動靜無常隨君上之
情欲者俗也斯二者非有品式條目之可
===
指非有形迹象類之可求而施於朝廷行
於天下貫乎人心關乎氣運者不可一日
而無焉故必有以提挈振舉于上導化移
易于下則天下之治可成不然雖事事而
核之人人而禁之力愈勞而其為治愈難
矣考之於古二帝之時不賞而勸不罰而
治三王之時不令而行不教而聽者良以
天子統三公三公率諸侯諸侯制卿大夫
卿大夫治士庶人紀綱正也耕者讓畔行

punctuated:
綱風俗者，上古之時無有也。自五子之歌，陶唐是載；棫樸之詠，文王是歌，而紀綱之名始立。書之風動，見于虞典；易之善俗，繋於周象，而風俗之名始著。盖綱猶網之有綱，紀猶絲之有紀。綱其大也，紀其小也。上行下效謂之風，衆心安定謂之俗。民函五常之性，剛柔緩急、音聲不同，繋水土之風氣者，風也；好惡取舍、動靜無常，隨君上之情欲者，俗也。斯二者，非有品式條目之可指，非有形迹象類之可求，而施於朝廷，行於天下，貫乎人心，關乎氣運者，不可一日而無焉。故必有以提挈振舉于上，導化移易于下，則天下之治可成。不然，雖事事而核之，人人而禁之，力愈勞而其為治愈難矣。
考之於古，二帝之時，不賞而勸，不罰而治；三王之時，不令而行，不教而聽者，良以天子統三公，三公率諸侯，諸侯制卿大夫，卿大夫治士庶人，紀綱正也。耕者讓畔，行
translation_en:
…governing order and popular customs did not exist in highest antiquity. Only when the Song of the Five Sons recorded Tao Tang, and the ode Luxuriant Oaks praised King Wen, did the term “governing order” first become established. The Documents speaks of people being stirred as by the wind in the Canon of Yu; the Changes speaks of improving customs in the Zhou Image commentaries. Thus the term “popular customs” first became prominent. Gang is like the main cord of a net, and ji like the ordering threads of silk: gang concerns the greater framework, ji its smaller particulars. What those above practice and those below imitate is called feng; that in which the hearts of the multitude rest content is called su. The people possess by nature the Five Constant Virtues, yet differ in firmness and gentleness, slowness and urgency, and the sounds of their voices. Such differences, tied to the influences of local waters and soil, are feng. Their likes and dislikes, choices and rejections, activity and repose have no fixed pattern, but follow the feelings and desires of their ruler: these are su. These two things—governing order and popular customs—have neither prescribed forms and itemized provisions that one can point to, nor visible traces and recognizable likenesses that one can seek out. Yet they operate at court, prevail throughout the realm, permeate human hearts, and bear upon the course of the vital forces. They cannot be dispensed with for even a day. Thus there must be means to uphold and invigorate governing order above, and to guide, transform, and reform customs below; then good government throughout the realm can be achieved. Otherwise, even if every affair is scrutinized and every person subjected to prohibitions, the greater the effort expended, the harder governing becomes.
Examining antiquity, we find that in the time of the Two Emperors people were encouraged without rewards and brought to order without punishments; in the time of the Three Kings they acted without commands and obeyed without instruction. This was truly because the Son of Heaven directed the Three Dukes, the Three Dukes led the regional lords, the regional lords controlled the ministers and grand masters, and the ministers and grand masters governed the servicemen and common people: governing order was properly maintained. Cultivators yielded the boundaries of their fields to one another, and travelers…

者讓路，士讓為大夫，大夫讓為卿，風俗同也。自時厥後，時異代殊。漢之初，以制度紀綱維持天下，不一再傳，而有指大如股、脛大如要，如賈誼所陳者。唐之初，欲明紀綱，為萬世法，及其季世，而有藩鎮阻兵、士卒逐帥，如司馬公所論者。宋之初，朝廷之令必行於轉運使，轉運使之令必行于州，州之令必行於縣，縣之令必行于吏民。迨于中葉，元帥畏偏裨，偏裨畏將校，將校畏士卒，至有一夫流言道路，而為之變令推恩，如司馬公所疏者。
大抵漢以規模為紀綱，唐以法令為紀綱，宋以忠孝廉耻為紀綱。其他若仲長統以井田、丁謹以賞罰、姚崇以官爵、杜黃裳以法度為紀綱者，各指一事言之，而非其全也。

translation_en:
…those traveling yielded the road; men of service yielded to others the position of grand master, and grand masters yielded to others the position of minister: customs were alike throughout the realm. Thereafter, times changed and dynasties differed. At the beginning of the Han, institutions and the framework of governing authority sustained the realm. Yet scarcely one or two successions later, there were fingers as large as thighs and shins as large as waists, as Jia Yi described. At the beginning of the Tang, the aim was to clarify the framework of governing authority and make it a model for all ages. By its final years, however, regional military commands relied on armed force to defy authority, and soldiers expelled their commanders, as Lord Sima discussed. At the beginning of the Song, the court’s orders were invariably carried out by the transport commissioners; the transport commissioners’ orders by the prefectures; the prefectures’ orders by the counties; and the counties’ orders by clerks and commoners. By the middle period, supreme commanders feared their subordinate commanders, subordinate commanders feared their officers, and officers feared their soldiers. It reached the point that a single man spreading rumors along the roads could cause orders to be changed and favors to be extended, as Lord Sima reported in a memorial.
Broadly speaking, the Han took its overall institutional arrangements as the framework of governing authority; the Tang took laws and ordinances; and the Song took loyalty, filial piety, integrity, and a sense of shame. Others identified this framework with particular things: Zhongchang Tong with the well-field system, Ding Jin [?] with rewards and punishments, Yao Chong with offices and ranks, and Du Huangshang with laws and institutions. Each spoke of a single aspect, rather than the whole.
Han customs were simple and sincere. Later, however, those who amassed wealth while holding office were regarded as outstanding men, and those who profited through wrongdoing as men of valor, as appears in Gong Yu’s words. Harshness was taken for discernment, severity for clear judgment, leniency for virtue, and heavy punishment for authority, as appears in an edict of Emperor Zhang.

唐之風俗素朴其後盧嘿因循者為清流

賢以犯顏敢諫為忠其後以恤民隱者為

之䟽以全身保位為賢以竭忠盡節為愚
以刻薄辦事為才以恬退自守為拙則見
於余應求之奏大抵漢之風俗尚經術尚

===

大夫博士宣帝遣太中大夫等循行風俗
則各因一事行之而非其本也我

國家
聖祖之所規畫
太宗之所考定內外相維體統不紊紀綱可謂
正矣今一事之施屢煩
詔旨一司之政頻費擿麾操筆有掣肘之虞
作舍有多言之惑若有異於前日之紀綱
punctuated:
唐之風俗素朴，其後盧嘿因循者為清流，行法蒞官者為俗吏，則見於憲宗之世。宋之風俗，以通經學古為高，以捄時行道為賢，以犯顏敢諫為忠。其後以恤民隱者為迂儒，以親庶務者為俗吏，則見於張叔夜之䟽；以全身保位為賢，以竭忠盡節為愚，以刻薄辦事為才，以恬退自守為拙，則見於余應求之奏。大抵漢之風俗尚經術、尚氣節，唐之風俗尚詞章，宋之風俗尚名檢。其間若武帝詔公卿、詔二千石，昭帝遣諫大夫、博士，宣帝遣太中大夫等循行風俗，則各因一事行之，而非其本也。
我國家，聖祖之所規畫，太宗之所考定，內外相維，體統不紊，紀綱可謂正矣。今一事之施，屢煩詔旨；一司之政，頻費揣摩。操筆有掣肘之虞，作舍有多言之惑，若有異於前日之紀綱。
translation_en:
Tang customs were simple and unadorned. Later, those who remained silent [?] and merely followed established routines were considered the pure-minded elite, while those who enforced the laws and discharged official duties were considered vulgar functionaries: this can be seen in the reign of Emperor Xianzong. Under the Song, mastery of the Classics and study of antiquity were esteemed as lofty attainments; remedying the troubles of the age and putting the Way into practice, as worthiness; and daring to remonstrate even at the risk of provoking the ruler’s anger, as loyalty. Later, those who cared about the people’s hidden sufferings were considered pedantic scholars, while those who personally attended to practical affairs were considered vulgar functionaries: this appears in Zhang Shuye’s memorial. Preserving oneself and retaining one’s position were considered worthy; exhausting one’s loyalty and fulfilling one’s integrity, foolish; handling affairs with harsh severity, capable; and quietly withdrawing and maintaining one’s principles, inept: this appears in Yu Yingqiu’s memorial. Broadly speaking, Han customs prized classical learning and moral courage; Tang customs prized literary composition; and Song customs prized reputation and disciplined conduct. Within these periods, Emperor Wu issued edicts to the highest ministers and officials of the two-thousand-bushel rank; Emperor Zhao dispatched Grand Masters of Remonstrance and Erudites; and Emperor Xuan dispatched Grand Masters of the Palace and others to make inspection tours concerning local customs. These measures were each undertaken in response to a particular matter, rather than addressing the root.
In our dynasty, what the Sagely Founder planned and Taizong examined and established ensures that officials within and outside the capital sustain one another and that the institutional hierarchy remains orderly. The governing framework may thus be called properly established. Now, however, implementing a single undertaking repeatedly troubles the throne for imperial directives, and administering a single office repeatedly requires laborious conjecture about intentions. Those who take up the brush fear that their elbows will be restrained; those who build a house are bewildered by a multitude of opinions. There seems to be a departure from the governing framework of earlier days.

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
累朝之所漸漬
列聖之所化導上下和洽遠邇齊同風俗可謂
一矣今醇厚者變而為澆漓剛勁者化而
為委靡爭進取則懷入市攫金之心工擠
排則為落穽下石之計若有異於前日之
風俗草野之下恒竊憂之而未敢以為言
也茲欲救偏補敝返朴而還淳者可不知
所本乎是故大臣者百官之表也
朝廷者四方之極也進賢退姦信賞必罰合
===
宮府為一體別尊卑為異秩有弗令令則
必行有弗謀謀則必斷韓昌黎之所謂存
國脉朱晦菴之所謂正人心者可行也紀
綱有弗正者乎獎恬抑競崇雅黜浮敦務
本實磨礪廉隅善則必表之以示勸惡則

punctuated:
累朝之所漸漬，列聖之所化導，上下和洽，遠邇齊同，風俗可謂一矣。今醇厚者變而為澆漓，剛勁者化而為委靡；爭進取則懷入市攫金之心，工擠排則為落穽下石之計，若有異於前日之風俗。草野之下，恒竊憂之，而未敢以為言也。茲欲救偏補敝，返朴而還淳者，可不知所本乎？
是故大臣者，百官之表也；朝廷者，四方之極也。進賢退姦，信賞必罰，合宮府為一體，別尊卑為異秩。有弗令，令則必行；有弗謀，謀則必斷。韓昌黎之所謂存國脉、朱晦菴之所謂正人心者，可行也。紀綱有弗正者乎？獎恬抑競，崇雅黜浮，敦務本實，磨礪廉隅。善則必表之以示勸，惡則必懲之以示戒。賈誼所述之四維、陸贄所陳之五術，可舉也。風俗有弗同者乎？
然又聞之，天下國家之本在身，君身者，紀綱風俗之所從以出也。愚不佞，倘得錄于執事
translation_en:
…Through the gradual influence of successive reigns and the transforming guidance of successive sage emperors, high and low lived in harmony, and near and far were alike: customs could indeed be called uniform. Now, however, sincerity and generosity have turned into shallow insincerity, and firmness and vigor have given way to listlessness. Those who compete for advancement harbor the impulse of a man who snatches gold in the marketplace; those skilled at squeezing others out devise schemes to throw stones upon someone who has fallen into a pit. Customs thus seem different from those of former days. From my humble position outside official life, I have constantly worried about this in private, yet have not ventured to speak of it. If we now wish to correct deviations and remedy abuses, to restore simplicity and return to sincerity, can we fail to understand the foundation on which this depends?
Thus, the great ministers are exemplars for all officials, and the court is the guiding pole for the four quarters. Advance the worthy and dismiss the wicked; make rewards trustworthy and punishments certain; unite the palace and the government as one body, while distinguishing superior and subordinate through their different ranks. An order need not be issued, but once issued it must be carried out; deliberation need not be undertaken, but once undertaken it must lead to a decision. What Han Changli called preserving the lifeblood of the state, and what Zhu Hui’an called rectifying people’s hearts, can then be put into practice. Could the governing order remain uncorrected? Reward those content to remain out of the limelight and restrain those who compete for advancement; honor refinement and reject frivolity; earnestly attend to fundamentals and substance, and cultivate integrity and moral principle. Good conduct must be publicly recognized to encourage others, and wrongdoing must be punished to warn them. The four bonds described by Jia Yi and the five methods set forth by Lu Zhi can then be implemented. Could customs fail to become uniform?
Yet I have also heard that the foundation of all under Heaven, the state, and the family lies in the person. The ruler’s own person is the source from which the governing order and customs proceed. Foolish and untalented as I am, if I should be selected by you, honored examiners …

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Supervising Secretary: 〔Candidates can sometimes know the attainments and careers of these Confucian scholars. 論前賢之所造詣必揆之道而後可以論
其人焉蓋前賢造詣之所在不可不審也
苟揆於道之所得而未能無疑則安能論
其人之所造而保其無舛乎執事發策以
前賢造詣為問其問大矣區區承學而敢
輕為之說哉雖然朱子以尚論古人為格
===
致之一端則亦有不容已者夫道中而已
過與不及其實恒均蓋不惟不底于大成
而其甚者且將陷於異端矣持此而論前
賢之造詣將不有得其萬一者乎横渠張
子之出與程子相望而龜山楊氏則受學
程子者也朱子有横渠似伯夷之論豈謂
其道之似哉其言曰二程之視横渠猶孔
子之視伯夷而不知孰可為程門之顏閔
也蓋以其道差次二程不當在弟子之列

考試官大學士李批：援據成說，折以己意，論四子者當矣。末復專以張子為師，尤見高識。

論前賢之所造詣，必揆之道，而後可以論其人焉。蓋前賢造詣之所在，不可不審也。苟揆於道之所得而未能無疑，則安能論其人之所造而保其無舛乎？執事發策，以前賢造詣為問，其問大矣。區區承學，而敢輕為之說哉？雖然，朱子以尚論古人為格致之一端，則亦有不容已者。夫道，中而已。過與不及，其實恒均。蓋不惟不底于大成，而其甚者且將陷於異端矣。持此而論前賢之造詣，將不有得其萬一者乎？横渠張子之出，與程子相望，而龜山楊氏則受學程子者也。朱子有横渠似伯夷之論，豈謂其道之似哉？其言曰：「二程之視横渠，猶孔子之視伯夷，而不知孰可為程門之顏閔也。」蓋以其道差次二程，不當在弟子之列，
translation_en:
…how tiresome are those who do not ground themselves in principle.

Comment by Examiner Li, Grand Secretary: He draws on established interpretations and weighs them with his own judgment; his assessments of the four masters are fitting. At the end, he singles out Master Zhang as his teacher, further demonstrating his exceptional discernment.

To discuss the attainments of earlier worthies, one must measure them against the Way; only then can one assess the men themselves. For the nature of their attainments must be carefully examined. If, when measuring what they attained against the Way, one still cannot resolve one’s doubts, how can one discuss their achievements and be certain of avoiding error? You gentlemen have issued a policy question asking about the attainments of earlier worthies. This is a weighty question indeed. How could an insignificant student such as I venture lightly to pronounce upon it? Nevertheless, Master Zhu regarded reaching back to assess the ancients as one aspect of investigating things and extending knowledge, so this is also something I cannot refrain from doing.

The Way is simply the mean. Going too far and falling short are, in substance, always equivalent. Not only do they fail to culminate in complete attainment; in their more extreme forms, they lead into heterodox teachings. If we use this standard to discuss the attainments of earlier worthies, might we not gain at least some small understanding of them?

Master Zhang of Hengqu emerged at much the same time as Master Cheng, while Yang of Guishan studied under Master Cheng. Master Zhu remarked that Hengqu resembled Bo Yi, but did he mean that their Ways were alike? He said: “The relationship of the two Cheng masters to Hengqu was like that of Confucius to Bo Yi; yet I do not know who could count as the Yan Hui and Min Ziqian of the Cheng school.” His point was that, in his attainment of the Way, Hengqu ranked somewhat below the two Cheng masters, but should not be placed among their disciples …

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
故擬之耳若胡文定論龜山之似展季則
有說焉龜山一出而當蔡京之日再出而
值南渡之初人有疑之者文定謂龜山之
出以救時也蔡氏安能浼之而朱子亦惜
其不大用于靖康則龜山之所以似展季
者有由然矣象山陸氏之興與朱子相友
而魯齋許氏則私淑朱子者也朱子有子
靜之學似禪之論盖象山自謂以孟子為
師欲先立乎其大者不甚究心于文義朱
===
子意其流弊將入于禪而不自知也若劉
靜脩論魯齋之疑于老則更有說焉魯齋
仕胡元之朝任斯道之重直以朱子為師
盖非無意于用夏變夷而靜脩謂其以一
身之利害節量天下之休戚著其說于退
齋記人公誦之則魯齋之所以疑于老者
亦有由矣夫四公豪傑之士曠世乃生而
其道之不一如此執事所謂後學亦徒因
古人之成說而未必真知之者誠是也然

translation_en:
…and it was only for this reason that he made the comparison. As for Hu Wending’s argument that Guishan resembled Zhan Ji, there is an explanation. Guishan first entered office in Cai Jing’s day, and entered office again at the beginning of the southward flight of the court. Some people questioned this. Wending held that Guishan entered office to rescue his age: how could Cai sully him? Master Zhu also regretted that his abilities had not been more fully employed during the Jingkang era. Thus there were grounds for Guishan’s resemblance to Zhan Ji.

When Lu Xiangshan rose to prominence, he was a friend of Master Zhu, while Xu Luzhai studied Master Zhu’s teachings without having been his personal disciple. Master Zhu argued that Zijing’s learning resembled Chan Buddhism. Xiangshan himself professed to take Mencius as his teacher and wished first to establish the greater part of himself, without devoting much attention to the meaning of texts. Master Zhu thought that the harmful tendencies of this approach would lead him into Chan without his realizing it.

As for Liu Jingxiu’s argument that Luzhai seemed akin to Laozi, there is a further explanation. Luzhai served at the court of the non-Han Yuan dynasty, shouldered the weighty responsibility of transmitting this Way, and took Master Zhu directly as his teacher. Presumably he was not without the intention of transforming the barbarians through Chinese civilization. Yet Jingxiu said that he measured the well-being and suffering of all under Heaven by the advantage or harm to his own person. He set out this view in his Record of the Retreat Studio, and people recited it openly. Thus there were also grounds for the suspicion that Luzhai resembled Laozi.

These four gentlemen were outstanding men, such as appear only once in many generations, yet their approaches to the Way differed in this manner. Your statement that later students merely follow the established judgments of earlier men without necessarily understanding them truly is indeed correct. Yet…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
以道之中而揆之則百步之射莫强其巧
力千里之謬實起于毫釐是豈可以無辨
哉是豈可以辨之弗明哉竊嘗論之橫渠
之所至幾于道之中矣而未底于大成後
學所當師而不敢議焉者也龜山之得于
程子者不為不深載道而南三傳而得朱
子其微詞奧義之存于書者可誦也其援
而止之而止則自處太高不幾于過中乎
象山晚歲追咎早年之粗心浮氣而加意
===
于窮理故朱子有去短集長之言盖其加
窮理之功于晚歲者可徵也其專于尊德
性而畧于道問學則自立太過不失于過
中乎魯齋之在當時道亦尊矣然其功業
之載史言語之行世門人弟子之得其傳
者視前賢之所樹立所講授中乎過乎抑
不及乎後學不能考而知也顧靜脩之論
魯齋出于同時本于獨見不於是取驗之
而又奚所屬乎盖承學之所得者如此不

punctuated: 以道之中而揆之，則百步之射，莫强其巧力；千里之謬，實起于毫釐。是豈可以無辨哉？是豈可以辨之弗明哉？竊嘗論之：橫渠之所至，幾于道之中矣，而未底于大成，後學所當師而不敢議焉者也。龜山之得于程子者，不為不深；載道而南，三傳而得朱子，其微詞奧義之存于書者可誦也。其援而止之而止，則自處太高，不幾于過中乎？象山晚歲追咎早年之粗心浮氣，而加意于窮理，故朱子有去短集長之言，盖其加窮理之功于晚歲者可徵也。其專于尊德性而畧于道問學，則自立太過，不失于過中乎？魯齋之在當時，道亦尊矣。然其功業之載史、言語之行世、門人弟子之得其傳者，視前賢之所樹立、所講授，中乎？過乎？抑不及乎？後學不能考而知也。顧靜脩之論魯齋，出于同時，本于獨見，不於是取驗之，而又奚所屬乎？盖承學之所得者如此，不
translation_en: …judged by the mean of the Way, however, in shooting a hundred paces one cannot force skill and strength; an error of a thousand li truly begins with a discrepancy of a hair’s breadth. How could these matters go undistinguished? How could one distinguish them without making the distinctions clear? I have ventured to consider them as follows. What Hengqu attained approached the mean of the Way, though he had not reached its full consummation. He is someone whom later students should take as their teacher and dare not criticize. What Guishan learned from Master Cheng was certainly profound. He carried the Way southward, and after three transmissions it reached Master Zhu. The subtle expressions and profound meanings preserved in his writings are worthy of recitation. Yet in his being drawn forward, then halted, and stopping [?], he placed himself too high: did this not verge on exceeding the mean? In his later years, Xiangshan reproached himself for the carelessness and restless disposition of his youth and devoted greater attention to investigating principle. Thus Master Zhu spoke of discarding shortcomings and gathering strengths. This provides evidence that Xiangshan increased his efforts to investigate principle in his later years. Yet by concentrating on honoring the moral nature while giving insufficient attention to inquiry and learning, he carried his independent stance too far: did he not err by exceeding the mean? In his own day, Luzhai’s Way was also honored. Yet if we compare his achievements recorded in history, his sayings circulating in the world, and the transmission received by his disciples with what earlier worthies established and taught, did he attain the mean, exceed it, or fall short? A later student such as myself cannot ascertain this through examination. Yet Jingxiu’s judgment of Luzhai came from a contemporary and rested on an independent insight. If we do not seek verification here, where else should we turn? Such, then, is what I have gained from pursuing learning. I do not…

translation_en:
…whether his understanding is mistaken or not. May you who preside recognize his commitment to the Way, though he has not yet been able to dispel his doubts, and kindly receive and instruct him.
Fourth Question
Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Chief Supervising Secretary: A policy essay sets forth plans. Testing candidates through policy essays reveals not only their learning but also the quality of their ability and judgment. In this script, the five policy essays answer the questions as readily as objects are poured from a bag, without laborious searching; the force of the writing and the inventiveness of its thought are extraordinary and unrestrained. The essay on name and substance directly addresses current affairs, and its proposals all hit the mark. At its close, it identifies the single word “sincerity” as the key to moving others and winning their trust. This may be called an argument that understands the root. Surely this is a scholar of broad learning and penetrating understanding! I did not expect to find such a man in the examination hall. In recommending him, I trust I shall not compromise the chief examiners’ reputation for discerning talent.
Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Hanlin Compiler: Others too have spoken of policies whose names endure while their substance has deteriorated. But in examining and testing the past and present, and bringing the argument to its essential conclusion—that achievements must be assessed and substantive results demanded—this script is exhaustive. Moreover, its exceptional ability and judgment, and its brilliant argumentation, appear in more than this one essay. If a student of the Classics such as this is recommended to His Majesty and later entrusted with office, surely his accomplishments will offer something worthy of admiration and fulfill people’s hopes?
Comment by Examiner Cheng, Hanlin Academician: All five policy essays display decisive judgment, and their writing is still more remarkable and imposing. The essay on name and substance is especially pertinent to current affairs, and for that reason it is included here. Discerning readers should understand…

有令而莫信下有志而莫伸展轉眩惑以
至于大壞極弊而後已爲治者可不審於
斯乎愚不遜于天下之事然執事之問及
之不可以不論也竊嘗聞之
祖宗之時上下之慱信内外之孚感終始之貞
固眞足以比隆前古之治矣及承平既久
民豐物豫文恬武嬉夷考其跡盖亦有名
實之不相應如執事所慮者姑舉一二言
punctuated:
其髙度尚不止此也。

考試官大學士本于批：此卷五策皆議論英發，才氣過人。披閲之餘，不勝賞歎。他日所就，知有未可量者。名實策尤剴切明當，卒歸于正，故特錄之，他不盡及也。

善為治者必先實而後名，善言治者必因名以考實。夫實之所在，名必隨之。然有有其實而名不彰者，有無其實而徒有其名者。天下之患，莫大於徇名而亡實。實之不足而徒徇其名，則毁譽亂真，刑賞失當，上有令而莫信，下有志而莫伸，展轉眩惑，以至于大壞極弊而後已。為治者可不審於斯乎？愚不通于天下之事，然執事之問及之，不可以不論也。竊嘗聞之，祖宗之時，上下之惇信，內外之孚感，終始之貞固，真足以比隆前古之治矣。及承平既久，民豐物豫，文恬武嬉，夷考其跡，盖亦有名實之不相應，如執事所慮者。姑舉一二言
translation_en:
…his lofty attainments extend still further than this.

Comment by Examiner and Grand Secretary Ben Yu 本于 [?]: All five policy essays in this script display brilliant argument and exceptional talent. Having read them, I cannot contain my admiration. His future achievements will, I believe, be beyond measure. The policy essay on names and realities is especially incisive, clear, and sound, and ultimately accords with what is right. It has therefore been selected for inclusion; the others are not included in full.

Those skilled in governing must put substance before name; those skilled in discussing government must examine substance through names. Where substance exists, a corresponding name will surely follow. Yet some possess the substance without their reputation becoming known, while others lack the substance and possess only the name. No affliction of the realm is greater than pursuing names and losing substance. When substance is lacking and names alone are pursued, praise and blame obscure the truth, punishments and rewards are improperly assigned, commands from above inspire no trust, and aspirations below find no fulfillment. Confusion compounds itself until utter ruin and the gravest abuses ensue. Can those who govern fail to examine this carefully? I am ignorant of the affairs of the realm, but since your question touches upon this matter, I cannot leave it undiscussed. I have heard that in the time of the imperial ancestors, the earnest trustworthiness of those above and below, the mutual confidence between those at court and those outside it, and their steadfast integrity from beginning to end truly sufficed to rival the flourishing government of antiquity. But after peace had long prevailed, the people were prosperous and goods abundant, while civil officials grew complacent and military officials idle. Upon calmly examining their conduct, one finds instances in which names and realities failed to correspond, just as you fear. Allow me to cite one or two examples and discuss…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
之審銓有籍而年地之冒詐相仍至有攘
文憑以假官秩者矣課績有狀而功過之
科條徒具至有易冊籍以避殿罰者矣芻
粟有勾稽侵盜者率諉之浥爛措空文以
為囷積者有之鹺貨有巡徼私市者率託
之官引鬻空名以獲息利者有之廩餼有
給役而黌校少絃誦之聲章印有辨驗而
文篆多摹刻之術託他姓以蔭官育市兒
以嗣秩嚴保勘而莫能止捕獲則張百成
===
千敗亡則減百為十詳審覈而不能禁招
伏有辭覆讞有案而情或不麗于法藝事
有役工物有直而名或不當其數察之者
愈詳而巧避之機屢出防之者愈密而潰
出之勢橫生是豈法之過哉亦嘗稽之昔
矣漢宣帝綜核名實欺謾之令雖下而王
成之偽增戶口蒙厚賞而不知光武責課
公卿督察之令屢頒而北狄尚疆屯田警
備亦多失實唐憲宗非不銳於為治也然

千敗輒則減百為十詳審覈而不能禁詰
伏有辭覆讞有察而情或不麗于法藝事
有役工物有直而名或不當其數察之者
愈詳而巧避之機屢出防之者愈密而潰
出之勢橫生是豈法之過哉亦嘗稽之昔
矣漢宣帝綜核名實欺謾之令雖下而王
成之僞增戶口蒙厚賞而不知光武責課
公卿督察之令屢頒而北狄尚彊屯田警
備亦多失實唐憲宗非不銳於為治也然
punctuated:
之。審銓有籍，而年地之冒詐相仍，至有攘文憑以假官秩者矣。課績有狀，而功過之科條徒具，至有易冊籍以避殿罰者矣。芻粟有勾稽，侵盜者率諉之浥爛，措空文以為囷積者有之。鹺貨有巡徼，私市者率託之官引，鬻空名以獲息利者有之。廩餼有給役，而黌校少絃誦之聲；章印有辨驗，而文篆多摹刻之術。託他姓以蔭官，育市兒以嗣秩，嚴保勘而莫能止。捕獲則張百成千，敗亡則減百為十，詳審覈而不能禁。招伏有辭，覆讞有案，而情或不麗于法；藝事有役，工物有直，而名或不當其數。察之者愈詳，而巧避之機屢出；防之者愈密，而潰出之勢橫生。是豈法之過哉？
亦嘗稽之昔矣。漢宣帝綜核名實，欺謾之令雖下，而王成之偽增戶口，蒙厚賞而不知。光武責課公卿，督察之令屢頒，而北狄尚疆，屯田警備亦多失實。唐憲宗非不銳於為治也，然
translation_en:
…these. There are registers for scrutinizing candidates for official appointment, yet false claims concerning age and native place persist; some even steal credentials to obtain official rank under false pretenses. There are written reports for evaluating performance, yet the categories of merit and fault exist merely in form; some even alter registers to evade penalties for poor performance. Fodder and grain are subject to accounting checks, yet embezzlers commonly attribute shortages to damp and rot; some pass off empty paperwork as stocks in granaries. The salt trade is patrolled, yet illicit traders commonly shelter behind official salt certificates; some sell nominal entitlements to reap profits. Stipends and provisions have personnel assigned to their distribution [?], yet little music or recitation is heard in the schools. Official seals undergo authentication, yet techniques for copying and carving their seal-script inscriptions abound. Some assume another surname to obtain office through hereditary privilege, or adopt a child from the marketplace to succeed to official rank. Strict guarantees and investigations cannot stop them. When reporting captures, they inflate a hundred into a thousand; when reporting losses in defeat, they reduce a hundred to ten. Detailed scrutiny and verification cannot prevent this. Confessions have written statements, and judicial reviews have case records, yet the circumstances sometimes fail to correspond to the law. Skilled work has assigned labor, and workmanship and materials have their prices, yet the stated items sometimes fail to match the quantities. The more detailed the scrutiny, the more frequently ingenious means of evasion emerge; the tighter the safeguards, the more breaches spring up unchecked. Can this be the fault of the laws?
I have also examined precedents from the past. Emperor Xuan of the Han comprehensively checked actual performance against nominal claims. Although he issued an edict against deception, Wang Cheng received lavish rewards for falsely inflating household and population figures, and the fraud went undetected. Emperor Guangwu held the highest officials accountable for their performance and repeatedly issued edicts requiring supervision and inspection; yet the northern Di remained powerful, and many reports concerning agricultural garrisons and defensive preparations likewise failed to reflect reality. Emperor Xianzong of the Tang was certainly zealous in governing, yet…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
邊軍之籍衣糧虛費交兵天德僅餘一弓
宋仁宗非不親庶政抑僥倖也然是非錯
謬賢不肖混淆而鈎校簿書訪尋比例非
政之實姦暴不除冤結不理而拘泥微文
糾察細過非刑之實材任相違職政廢弛
而檢勘出身比類資序非審官之實乆大
之謀棄而不省淺近之言應時施行非納
諫之實司馬光蓋責備焉實則聚斂而名
曰理財用實則掊剋而名曰抑兼并實則
===
開邊而名曰討不庭實則尚同而名曰一
衆志移囚外舍而奏囹圄空虛水旱不以
聞而稱大有年諫諍路塞則曰無事可言
賢才盡廢則曰野無遺伏胡寅有是論矣
噫豈獨一時一事然哉獨慨夫四君者皆
有願治之心而所謂綜核責課者未臻其
效也為今之計豈能舍綜核責課之法而
聽其所至哉亦於是而務求其實耳一政
之施堅如金石一令之出信如四時示好

曰理財開實則掊剋而名曰抑兼并實則
===
開邊而名曰討不庭實則尚同而名曰一
衆志移因外舍而奏囹圄空虛水旱不以
聞而稱大有年讒諍路塞則曰無事可言
賢才盡廢則曰野無遺伏胡寅有是論矣
噫豈獨一時一事然哉獨慨夫四君者皆
有願治之心而所謂綜核責課者未臻其
效也為今之計豈能舍綜核責課之法而
聽其所至哉亦於是而務求其實耳一政
之施堅如金石一令之出信如四時示好
punctuated:
邊軍之籍，衣糧虛費；交兵天德，僅餘一弓。宋仁宗非不親庶政、抑僥倖也，然是非錯謬，賢不肖混淆，而鈎校簿書、訪尋比例，非政之實；姦暴不除，冤結不理，而拘泥微文、糾察細過，非刑之實；材任相違，職政廢弛，而檢勘出身、比類資序，非審官之實；乆大之謀棄而不省，淺近之言應時施行，非納諫之實。司馬光蓋責備焉。實則聚斂，而名曰理財用；實則掊剋，而名曰抑兼并；實則開邊，而名曰討不庭；實則尚同，而名曰一衆志；移囚外舍，而奏囹圄空虛；水旱不以聞，而稱大有年；諫諍路塞，則曰無事可言；賢才盡廢，則曰野無遺伏。胡寅有是論矣。
噫！豈獨一時一事然哉？獨慨夫四君者皆有願治之心，而所謂綜核責課者未臻其效也。為今之計，豈能舍綜核責課之法，而聽其所至哉？亦於是而務求其實耳。一政之施，堅如金石；一令之出，信如四時；示好
translation_en:
…Yet the frontier army’s muster rolls entailed wasteful expenditure on clothing and provisions; when battle was joined at Tiande, only a single bow remained [?]. Emperor Renzong of the Song did personally attend to the many affairs of government and curb those seeking unmerited advantage. Yet right and wrong were confused, and the worthy were indiscriminately mixed with the unworthy. Checking registers and documents and searching out comparable precedents did not constitute the substance of government. The wicked and violent were not removed, and grievances were not redressed; clinging to minute provisions and investigating petty faults did not constitute the substance of penal administration. Abilities and appointments were mismatched, and official duties fell into neglect; scrutinizing qualifications for entry into office and comparing ranks of seniority did not constitute the substance of evaluating officials. Plans of lasting and far-reaching benefit were discarded without consideration, while shallow proposals promising immediate results were put into effect; this did not constitute the substance of accepting remonstrance. Sima Guang indeed reproached these failings.
In reality they amassed wealth through exaction, but called it managing financial resources; in reality they squeezed the people, but called it curbing the concentration of wealth; in reality they expanded the frontiers, but called it punishing those who failed to acknowledge imperial authority; in reality they prized conformity, but called it unifying the people’s will. They moved prisoners to quarters outside the prison and then reported that the cells were empty. They withheld reports of floods and droughts and proclaimed a year of abundant harvests. When the avenues of remonstrance were blocked, they said there was nothing to speak of; when all the worthy and talented had been cast aside, they said no worthy men remained undiscovered outside official service. Hu Yin made this criticism.
Alas! Could this have been true of only one time or one affair? What is especially lamentable is that all four rulers desired good government, yet their purported comprehensive scrutiny and enforcement of official accountability failed to achieve their intended effect. In planning for the present, how could we abandon these methods and let matters take whatever course they might? We must instead strive through them to secure substantive results. Let the implementation of each policy be firm as metal and stone; let the issuance of each command be dependable as the four seasons; make manifest what is approved…

惡之公，明賞罰之正，慎忠偽之辨，嚴勤惰之别，不數年而天下之政可歸于實也。若徒取辦於文字之粗，錄功於齒頰之末，則荀悅所謂虛偽誣罔者，安保其必無，而豈戴記之所謂忠信誠愨者哉？抑為政之道，必本乎誠。上以誠感，下以誠應，存省於念慮之微，而檢察於蹈履之際，實周於施行之地，而孚結於觀感之餘，則忠可以貫金石，信可以及豚魚，而況於人乎？況於天下之事乎？是固為政者之所當盡心焉者也。執事倘不以為迂而忽之，幸甚。

translation_en:
…impartiality in dislikes; make clear the rectitude of rewards and punishments, take care in distinguishing loyalty from deceit, and strictly distinguish diligence from indolence. Within a few years, the governance of the realm can return to substantive achievement. If, however, one merely seeks to discharge duties through superficial paperwork and records accomplishments on the strength of mere words, how can one guarantee the absence of what Xun Yue called falsehood and deception? And how could this constitute what the Record of Dai calls loyalty, trustworthiness, sincerity, and integrity?
Moreover, the way of governing must be rooted in sincerity. Those above move others through sincerity, and those below respond with sincerity. If one preserves and examines one's mind in the subtlest stirrings of thought, scrutinizes one's conduct in practice, brings genuine substance to every act of administration, and wins lasting trust through the example others perceive, then loyalty can penetrate metal and stone, and trustworthiness can reach even pigs and fish. How much more, then, can they reach human beings—and the affairs of the realm! This is assuredly what those who govern ought to devote their whole hearts to. I would count myself most fortunate if you, sir, did not dismiss these words as impractical.
Fifth Question
Lun Wenxu

同考試官編修徐批：兵民一策，能言者多，但鮮有灼然可施於今而垂於後者。此篇於國初創制之善與今日所欲復初之意，歷述無遺，且其終畫弛張之迂不則是，豈一日心思所及？因言察實，度其繫人望也久矣。
考試官學士程批：禮闈第一人，甚難其選。晚得此卷，同然一辭。五策中已錄其一，而惠民畧兵之對尤有歸重，故并錄之。
考試官大學士李批：此篇詞意懇到，宜有深於心而形之乎言，非苟焉應答者，並不厭重錄。
為國者當惠民以實其內，尤當養兵以固其外。蓋兵與民，有國者所恃以安而不可忽焉者也。苟不知所以惠之與所以養之，而求治效于天下，可得哉？執事先生發策，以是為問，其所以為天下計也大矣。布衣
translation_en:
…benefits sagely governance. From this alone one can judge his learning for practical service in the world.
Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Compiler: Many can discuss the policy question concerning soldiers and the people, but few offer proposals clearly practicable today and worthy of transmission to later generations. This essay recounts exhaustively both the merits of the institutions established at the dynasty’s founding and the present intention to restore those original arrangements. Moreover, its concluding plans for relaxing and tightening measures [?]—could these have been conceived in a single day? Examining the substance through his words, I judge that he has long been a man upon whom others place their hopes.
Comment by Examiner Cheng, Academician: Selecting the first-ranked candidate in the Metropolitan Examination is exceedingly difficult. We obtained this script late in the process and unanimously agreed upon it. One of his five policy essays has already been included, but his response concerning benefiting the people and military management [?] is especially sound in its priorities, so we include it as well.
Comment by Examiner Li, Grand Secretary: This essay is earnest and thorough in both wording and thought. Surely these ideas lie deep in his heart and find expression in his words; this is no perfunctory response. We therefore do not object to including another of his essays.
Those who govern a state should benefit the people to strengthen it internally, and should especially provide for the troops to secure it externally. For troops and people are what a ruler relies upon for peace, and neither may be neglected. If one does not understand how to benefit the people and provide for the troops, can one expect effective government throughout the realm? You gentlemen administering the examination have posed a policy question on this subject: far-reaching indeed is your concern for the realm. A commoner…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
之士惡足以語此然竊聞之人情莫不欲
富三王厚之而不困人情莫不欲逸三王
節其力而不盡故足以祈天永命而致泰
和之治焉然則惠民養兵之說又孰有易
此兩端者哉洪惟我
太祖高皇帝之受命啓運也取天下之民而歸
之版籍收天下之兵而納之尺伍其惠之
也不傷其財而養之也不盡其力故民樂
于供賦兵堅于捍衛蓋以三代之心行三
===
代之政有非漢唐宋之所能及者以今視
昔承平久矣民之轉徙者相踵而藏匿山
澤者時懼其不逞兵之逃亡者相望而戰
戍四境者恒憂其不足
列聖嗣統每切注意增有司以專撫民之事矣
惠雖周而民不加多責憲臣以督清軍之
政矣法雖嚴而兵不加衆何邪蓋
國初賦既輕而吏多廉在版籍者但知享安
土之樂而已工不繁而將多良在尺伍者

punctuated:
之士，惡足以語此？然竊聞之：人情莫不欲富，三王厚之而不困；人情莫不欲逸，三王節其力而不盡。故足以祈天永命，而致泰和之治焉。然則惠民養兵之說，又孰有易此兩端者哉？洪惟我太祖高皇帝之受命啓運也，取天下之民而歸之版籍，收天下之兵而納之尺伍。其惠之也，不傷其財；而養之也，不盡其力。故民樂于供賦，兵堅于捍衛。蓋以三代之心，行三代之政，有非漢唐宋之所能及者。
以今視昔，承平久矣。民之轉徙者相踵，而藏匿山澤者，時懼其不逞；兵之逃亡者相望，而戰戍四境者，恒憂其不足。列聖嗣統，每切注意，增有司以專撫民之事矣，惠雖周而民不加多；責憲臣以督清軍之政矣，法雖嚴而兵不加衆，何邪？蓋國初賦既輕而吏多廉，在版籍者但知享安土之樂而已；工不繁而將多良，在尺伍者
translation_en:
…a scholar without office—how could I be qualified to speak of this? Yet I have heard that all people desire prosperity: the Three Kings enriched them without impoverishing them. All people desire ease: the Three Kings used their strength sparingly without exhausting it. Thus they could pray to Heaven for an enduring mandate and bring about an age of supreme harmony. In discussions of benefiting the people and sustaining the troops, what could supersede these two principles? Let us reverently consider how our Emperor Taizu Gao, upon receiving the mandate and inaugurating his reign, entered the people of the realm in household registers and enrolled its soldiers in military ranks [?]. In benefiting the people, he did not deplete their wealth; in sustaining the troops, he did not exhaust their strength. Thus the people gladly paid their taxes, and the soldiers stood firm in defense. With the spirit of the Three Dynasties, he practiced the government of the Three Dynasties, achieving what the Han, Tang, and Song could not match.
Comparing the present with the past, we have long enjoyed peace. Yet people who move away follow one another in succession, and there is continual fear that those hiding in the mountains and marshes will turn to lawlessness. Soldiers desert in an unending stream, while there is constant concern that those fighting and garrisoning the frontiers are too few. The successive sage emperors, on inheriting the throne, have paid close attention to these matters. They have increased the number of responsible officials to devote themselves to caring for the people; yet although their beneficence reaches everywhere, the people do not increase in number. They have charged censorial officials with supervising the verification of military rolls; yet although the laws are strict, the troops do not increase in number. Why is this? At the founding of the dynasty, taxes were light and officials were mostly incorruptible, so those entered in the household registers knew only the pleasure of dwelling securely on their land. Labor demands were not excessive, and commanders were mostly capable, so those enrolled in the military ranks [?]…

title: 弘治十二年會試錄
text:
但知盡拱衞之誠而已而又奚求哉况先
王之制民也使之出賦稅以給公上而均
需雜征之出于近時者十倍於昔孰有為
之懇減而蘇其困乎豈惟無之且假託以
為利若之何其不轉徙也先王之制兵也
使之負干戈以衞社稷而公作私役之興
于比歲者諸路相仍孰有為之恤存而惜

===

之財僅足供一歲之用萬一水旱不常其
何以為繼乎仰給之地如此而况他郡乎
三邊之兵雖若素整而力之所責效者疲
矣顧猶值夫夷狄中衰屯邊之卒亦僅足
支一方之虞萬一戎心叵測其何以為禦
乎要害之地如此而况他鎮乎是不能不
廑
